News.title: Body found in search for missing three-year-old Noah Woods
News.content:
Supt Pearse said formal identification had yet to take place, but Noah's family had been informed.

"Our thoughts are with Noah's family and all those who knew him," he said.

"We have been overwhelmed by the outpouring of public support and people putting on their boots to help."

Police said at least 1,300 members of the public had helped in the search for the missing boy, who was non-verbal and partially deaf.

People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire had turned up to help.

Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the estuary of the River Stour on the Essex border.

Volunteer efforts had been co-ordinated from Brantham Leisure Centre and the village hall, which ran out of hi-vis vests due to the number of volunteers.

Those looking for Noah had been told he would not respond to shouting.

News.title: Charles said Diana would be forgotten 'soon enough', Earl Spencer claims in book
News.content:
Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed King Charles said "we'll forget her soon enough" days after her death, in an extract from his upcoming memoir published by the Daily Mail.

He claimed the then-Prince of Wales subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he insisted Diana would not have wanted Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to have to walk in her funeral procession.

Buckingham Palace has strongly pushed back against the claim.

A spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. BBC News has not seen the book in full.

In the first extract, external from it to be made public, Earl Spencer claims to have been informed by a senior Palace aide that the young princes would walk alongside Princess Diana's coffin, which he objected to.

He claims to have received a phone call from Charles shortly after.

Earl Spencer wrote in the book: "He [Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough'."

Earl Spencer's book about his sister seems set to open a very difficult time in the recent history of the Royal Family.

The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, in a car crash in 1997, had created a volatile atmosphere, in which the royals were accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and had seemed out of touch with the public mood.

Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's untimely death.

Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do".

In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day.

Earlier on Wednesday, it emerged that copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book had been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands.

BBC News understands four copies of the Dutch language edition were taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher's printers to their warehouse.

News.title: 'Putney pusher' suspect found dead at home
News.content:
The man suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a bus during a run on Putney Bridge in west London in 2017, has been found dead at his home.

Nicholas Brandram, 44, was under investigation in the so-called "Putney pusher" case, after CCTV went viral showing just how close the woman came to being run over by the 430 bus, in a seemingly unprovoked attack.

He was arrested in June this year on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. Last week, the Metropolitan Police confirmed he had been released under investigation.

The banker was found dead in his home on Tuesday evening. The Met said his death was being treated as "unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious".

News.title: Watch: BBC crew catch thieves in act while filming shoplifting report
News.content:
A BBC team who came to a Greggs to talk to staff and customers about shoplifting were confronted by thieves openly stealing in front of them.

Two men with rucksacks did not bother to hide their faces as they ransacked the fridge for more, swearing angrily at a female worker who tried to stop them, at the outlet in Bearwood, near Birmingham.

Workers told the BBC the brazen 55-second raid was all in a day's work, with offenders targeting the outlet multiple times every day.

Greggs says it takes the industry-wide problem of shoplifting "extremely seriously", has enhanced security measures across its outlets and works closely with police.

News.title: How being music's Mr Nice Guy contributed to biggest crisis of Ed Sheeran's career
News.content:
Singer Ed Sheeran is facing the biggest controversy of his career after a storm over a decision to drop support act Macklemore from his US stadium tour following the rapper's on-stage pro-Palestinian comments.

Sheeran is one of the most successful songwriters of all time. He has sold more than 120 million records and spent more than 1,000 weeks on the US album charts.

Part of his appeal - apart from those insidiously catchy songs - is his everyman persona. He looks and dresses like a fan on the train home from Glastonbury, rather than one of the festival's headliners.

He has carefully cultivated a non-threatening, everyone welcome public image. In 2014, he donated his entire wardrobe to charity shops. The same year, he adopted a one-month-old kitten, saving it from euthanasia, and named it Graham. Today, he runs a charity providing music lessons to under-18s in his home county of Suffolk.

He tries to stay out of politics - usually only getting involved to campaign for issues like copyright protection and ticket touting, or to raise concerns over the impact of Brexit on touring musicians.

But like most artists, he leans left. In 2017, he said he supported then-Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, despite not endorsing him at the stump.

"People thought that, because I didn't put myself behind him, I wasn't a Corbyn supporter," Sheeran told the Sunday Times. "If you knew me as a person, and listened to my music, you would be able to make a pretty educated guess that he would be the kind of person I really dig."

When it comes to non-musical issues, Sheeran prefers to remain circumspect. His reasoning, he says, is that music should unite. He views his concerts as a "place of safety and sanctuary" built on shared humanity.

This week, that argument has come crumbling down - creating a crisis for his reputation and career.

News.title: US House votes to hold billionaire Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt
News.content:
The US House of Representatives has agreed to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for defying legal summons related to its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Black - who had business ties to Epstein - did not comply with a subpoena ordering him to appear before the House Oversight Committee earlier this month and share documents related to Epstein.

Lawyers for Black, who has sued over the summons, called the contempt move "outrageous".

After passage of the measure holding Black in contempt, Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer said: "No one is above the law."

"We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors."

In a statement shared with US media, lawyers for Black called the House move an "outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr. Black".

"The full House is holding him in contempt without any regard to the active litigation challenging the lawfulness of the Committee's actions and the ethics complaint against Chairman Comer," they said.

The measure, which passed by unanimous consent, means the matter will be referred to the US justice department, which will decide whether to criminally prosecute Black.

In a statement, the committee's top Democrat, Congressman Robert Garcia, called the contempt vote "an important step towards justice and accountability".

"We will continue to center the survivors in our fight to hold those responsible for these horrific crimes," he said.

Black walked out of voluntary testimony before the House Oversight Committee in June after he was asked about nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) he may have signed, lawmakers said at the time.

Black left Apollo Global Management, which he co-founded, amid scrutiny in 2021 over his Epstein ties. He has denied any wrongdoing with regards to his dealings with Epstein.

The subpoenas, which ordered Black to share NDAs and give an on-camera deposition under oath, were issued after he left the committee meeting in June.

Black has said he hired Epstein as a wealth management adviser, telling lawmakers in June that he gave Epstein $158m (Â£118m) for legitimate reasons.

The billionaire has said he did not know about Epstein's crimes until he was charged with sex trafficking in July 2019.

News.title: 'Let's go, let's go' - inside catastrophic Manchester derby VAR mistake
News.content:
Pro Ref has placed a huge level of training and resources into VAR in an attempt to make it as efficient and accurate as possible.

But when an error of this magnitude happens, no amount of investment can mask the failure.

There have been calls to appoint VAR specialists, yet this is exactly what Donohue is - in the Premier League's definition.

Three seasons ago, Pro Ref asked for candidates interested in becoming video officials.

All those who applied were put through aptitude tests. About 15 made it through to the final stages of training, of which 10 have officiated games in the Premier League.

One of those is Donohue, who on Sunday was the video official for the 65th time.

Such as been Donohue's development that he is now on the international list, appointed to Uefa club competition qualifying ties over the summer.

Donohue has made mistakes, in fact very few do not. It shows how difficult the role is.

The only two VARs to have a clear record over the last two seasons are Nick Hopton and Neil Davies, both graduates from the same accelerated programme.

Persuading referees to hang up their whistles and spend their professional lives in the VAR room is not easy, nor does it guarantee success.

Lee Mason and Mike Dean, the Premier League's only full-time VARs appointed after retirement, were both dismissed by Webb just a few months into his tenure because of a catalogue of errors.

One of the only leagues which has a full team of officials who only act as VARs and never go out on the pitch is Spain's La Liga and second division - yet one glance at the headlines there will tell you the controversy is no different to that in England.

At the start of last season the VAR completely missed that a player who scored a goal was in an offside position when the ball was played.

Pro Ref will have questions to answer over its processes and why a VAR is rushing so desperately over a review in one of the biggest games of the season.

That did not happen when West Ham's stoppage-time equaliser against Arsenal was ruled out last season. It took over four minutes - but the VAR came to the correct outcome.

The obsession with speed threatens to undermine all the work behind the scenes.

But that feels like a football problem and not one caused solely by the actions of the VAR.

News.title: British soldier who died in Ukraine road accident named by MoD
News.content:
The member of the UK armed forces who died in a road traffic accident in Ukraine last week has been named as Major Paul Wilks.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) described the 40-year-old as a "gifted leader who earned the admiration and respect of all those fortunate enough to have served alongside him".

The incident on Saturday was not the result of hostile action, the BBC understands, with the MoD stating that the accident happened "away from the front lines".

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Major Wilks served this country with pride and dedication. His loss will be deeply felt by those around him."

He said: "The tributes paid by those who worked with Paul illustrate his exceptional talent and ability, underscored by genuine warmth, compassion and a desire to support others.

"His loss is a poignant reminder of the enormous sacrifice that our armed forces and their families make in the service of our country."

Major Wilks, described by the MoD as a "proud family man", is survived by his wife and two sons.

He joined the Intelligence Corps in 2012 and was deployed on multiple operational tours, including to Afghanistan.

Major Wilks was the recipient of two operational service medals and a long service and good conduct medal.

His commanding officer praised Major Wilks as "a man of great intellect, yet he remained a mate to those he served with".

They added: "He spoke often of his love for his wife and two sons, expressing his deep gratitude for the support they provided, which allowed him to serve with such distinction.

"It is because of that foundation that he was able to meet the challenges of his role, and it is in the course of his devotion to duty that he made the ultimate sacrifice."

News.title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike
News.content:
Schools in England are to get around Â£500 million in extra funding towards the teachers' pay award this school year, reducing the risk of a strike ballot by the largest education union.

Schools had been expected to fund some of the 3.5% teachers pay increase for the current school year out of their existing budgets, which National Education Union (NEU) leaders had strongly objected to.

Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the NEU, said the offer of more funding was a "significant" step in negotiations.

In a letter to the union on Wednesday, which has been seen by the BBC, the government said the increase would be funded by savings in employers' contributions to the local government pension scheme.

The letter said the 4.9 percentage point drop in what employers are expected to contribute will deliver "significant savings" on the pay bill for support staff, which will not be clawed back by central government.

The National Education Union said it expected the extra money to be around Â£500m, which schools can now use towards teachers' pay this year.

In July, ministers accepted the recommendation of the independent pay review body for teachers and agreed a 3.5% increase from September 2026 would be followed by 3% the following year.

The pay increase had been partly funded by an additional Â£700m for 2026-27 and Â£1.1bn for the following year.

Independent economists at the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said that left schools facing a shortfall of around 1% between rising costs and funding this year.

Luke Sibieta, IFS research fellow, said the extra money would mean the pay increase this year was fully funded - and on top of other funding increases, schools would be Â£1.6bn better off by next year than they had expected this summer.

The additional money could potentially bring the uplift for this year into line with next year.

Kebede said schools has been "running on empty" and the funding signalled "a welcome return to reality, and a message of hope for the entire school community".

Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the National Association of Headteachers, said the decision is "certainly welcome", putting schools in a "better position".

He said his union would look carefully at the detail "to determine whether this means the pay uplift is genuinely fully funded" for schools.

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said he was "pleased" at the announcement of additional funding but "the wider pressure on school and college budgets remains intense".

Similarly, the NASUWT union welcomed the news. General secretary Matt Wrack added schools needed "a sustainable, long-term injection of extra funding" to meet the needs of young people.

In an indicative ballot by the NEU in April, 90% of teachers who voted said they would be prepared to take industrial action over funding and pay, on a turnout of 48%.

A formal ballot was due to begin on 3 October and close 15 December, raising the prospects of teachers pay strikes early in 2027.

The national executive of the NEU will meet on 24 September to consider whether to call that off following the additional funding on offer from the government.

A spokesperson for Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the government was "confident schools can now meet the costs of the award at a national level".

"The Secretary of State has been clear from day one that supporting teacher recruitment, retention and wellbeing, and rebuilding the relationship with the profession, are among her top priorities."

Laura Trott, shadow education secretary, said it was "not at all clear this is new money for schools", and questioned whether schools were "simply being given funding to replace savings they had already built into their budgets".

Liberal Democrat schools spokesperson Caroline Voaden said she was "glad the government has seen sense, but schools shouldn't have gone through the stress of working out where the money would come from".

News.title: Village votes to leave UK over asylum housing plan in symbolic referendum
News.content:
Residents of an Oxfordshire village have voted to become independent from the UK in a symbolic referendum held in protest at plans to house more than 1,000 migrants at a former military base.

Villagers in Piddington, near Bicester, voted on Tuesday over Home Office proposals to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at nearby MoD Bicester.

The referendum was organised by the parish council and out of 312 votes cast, 285 voted to leave, 26 voted no, and one ballot paper was spoiled.

The culture secretary told BBC Breakfast the government would not reconsider the migrant housing proposal.

Piddington's 350 residents were invited to cast their ballot in a small box outside the village hall.

Delivering the result, parish council vice chair Susannah Parden said: "We are Piddington the village that roars."

Parish council chair Tim McNally added: "This is an example of democracy in operation.

"We went into this village hall as the underdogs - we had a plucky idea. We have given a message to the world."

News.title: Police officer guilty of series of rapes and sex attacks over 17 years
News.content:
A former Police Scotland officer has been convicted of a catalogue of sex crimes, including two counts of rape, over a 17-year period.

Campbell Petrie, 50, was found guilty of nine charges at the High Court in Glasgow, which took place between 2006 and 2023.

Petrie was a serving officer at the time of the offences, which included indecent assault, assault with intent to rape and assault to injury and danger of life.

The force confirmed he was arrested, charged and suspended from duty in December 2023. He retired from the force in December last year.

Petrie was remanded in custody and is due to be sentenced next month.

News.title: Ex-BBC presenter questions role of Royal Family in new documentary
News.content:
Veteran broadcaster John Humphrys has said the people of the United Kingdom should "be able to choose our leaders" as he releases a documentary exploring the role of the Royal Family.

Humphrys, who for decades was one of the most prominent faces on the BBC, is presenting a new Channel 4 documentary called The Royals: Time to Go?

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast, the Cardiff-born presenter said he "admires" King Charles III in many ways, but said it was a "matter of choice".

Buckingham Palace has been approached for comment.

In the documentary, Humphrys speaks to both critics and supporters of the monarchy, and makes the case for electing a president as the head of state.

He recalled seeing the late Queen Elizabeth II visiting Cardiff when he was growing up, watching her being driven down Newport Road.

"My father didn't attend and said he would never bend the knee to anyone. I guess that rubbed off on me," he said.

Humphrys asked why it was seen as such a taboo to call for an alternative to the Royal Family, saying that "we can because it's a democracy".

"I know the monarch is not a political leader, but he is our leader, and we need to bow our knee to him.

"That's what I object to. Shouldn't we get a choice?"

He met the Queen throughout his career, including at Buckingham Palace where he said he spoke to her "and the corgis of course".

Humphrys, who presented the Nine O'Clock News, the Today programme and Mastermind throughout a decades-long career with the corporation, said he took the opportunity to ask her for an interview.

"When I'd finished, she looked up at me and said just one word 'no' and I thought I could build on that," he said.

News.title: More than £2m spent by government on influencers since July 2024
News.content:
While the figures cover Labour's time in office under Sir Keir Starmer, his successor Andy Burnham has continued to use influencers to get the government's message out.

On his first day as prime minister, Burnham was already posting videos on TikTok of him running with Sir Mo Farah and appearing on influencer Max Klymenko's "career ladder" podcast.

Prof Andrew Chadwick, an expert in political communication at Loughborough University, said working with influencers "chimes with the change of direction since Burnham took over", with the PM using his following on TikTok and Instagram to engage directly with the public.

He argued using influencers could be an effective way of telling the public about things like how to file their taxes, or counter health misinformation on social media.

Governments have traditionally paid for advertising through newspapers, TV, radio and social media.

But Prof Chadwick says paying content creators is increasingly used on top of this.

At a time when more people - especially younger age groups - are switching off from traditional media, he said influencers could act as a trusted source of information.

"It's taken a while to get to this stage, but I'm surprised in a sense at how little has been spent by these departments," he added.

However, Prof Chadwick said there were also risks, as the government had less control over what posts could appear alongside, which could damage credibility.

He added that it was difficult to predict what the public response would be to a collaboration.

"The comments are there, they're underneath the post, and you'll get these kind of backlash moments," he said.

"That undermines the purpose of the original campaign."

Earlier this year, the Department for Education faced criticism over its collaboration with reality TV star Gemma Collins to promote post-16 education.

The department said Collins was not paid for the content.

Defending the campaign, then-education secretary Bridget Phillipson said Collins could reach people politicians could not, suggesting some of the criticism was driven by "snobbery".

Government guidelines for influencer marketing have existed since 2023.

Under the government's influencer due diligence policy, external, departments must consider the size and demographics of an influencer's following, as well as whether they have previously posted about political issues which could undermine the effectiveness of a campaign.

Spending by government departments on social media influencers since July 2024:

Department for Education: Â£718,971 (from 2024/25 to July 2026)

HMRC: Â£591,200 (excludes agency fees)

Department for Transport: Â£302,873.83

Department for Work and Pensions: Â£212,425

Ministry of Justice: Â£206,140

Department for Energy Security and Net Zero: Â£176,100

Ministry of Defence: Â£123,173

Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government: Â£114,831.95

Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade: Â£39,700

Departments including the Treasury and the Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs said they did not spend any money on social media influencers during the period.

Some departments, such as the Home Office and Foreign Office, said they did not hold information on payments to influencers centrally.

News.title: Call to raise tax thresholds among union demands ahead of Budget
News.content:
Unions who donate to Labour will meet John Healey on Thursday to press home their demands ahead of next month's Budget.

Unite, the UK's second biggest union, has called for a reversal of the freezing of tax thresholds, that see the lowest paid drawn into paying tax.

The union's leader, Sharon Graham, said she told Andy Burnham that the cut to the winter fuel allowance, carried out under former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, was a "disgrace", adding: "What to you need to do is winter fuel in reverse - something that says to everyday people I am on your side."

The call is one of a number of policy proposals unions are taking to the chancellor, including increased taxes on tech companies.

Unions say they believe Healey's first budget will define Andy Burnham's direction of travel as prime minister.

Unite took legal action against Sir Keir's government when the winter fuel payment was restricted to the poorest pensioners, and Graham believed this policy - which was not in Labour's manifesto - was politically poisonous.

Burnham said the freezing of tax thresholds had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to return to Westminster as MP for Makerfield.

In her last Budget, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves froze tax thresholds until 2031. The basic rate of 20% is paid on annual earnings between Â£12,571 and Â£50,270. The higher rate of 40% is paid on earnings between Â£50,271 and Â£125,140.

By not uprating those rates in line with inflation, more lower paid people have paid tax for the first time and more better-off workers, including public service workers such as senior nurses, police officers and teachers, are now paying tax at the higher rate.

Graham said: "We must see things happen immediately. I told him [Burnham] that you have to make working class people believe their best days are in front of them.

"That tax threshold of around Â£12,500 - if that hadn't been frozen for the past few years it would have moved up to over Â£16,000 now. People at the lower end are paying eye-watering amounts of tax."

News.title: Ex-officer jailed over 'toxic' WhatsApp culture
News.content:
An ex-police sergeant who asked to share a female suspect's sex video with "the lads from footy" has been jailed for four years.

Former Cambridgeshire Police officer Paul Street, 41, engaged in "salacious gossip" with former PC Josh Williams after he found intimate pictures and footage on the woman's personal phone.

The Old Bailey heard how Street, of Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, created a "toxic" WhatsApp culture at work. He was found guilty of two charges of misconduct in a public office.

Judge Mark Lucraft KC said: "The public should expect to be able to trust police officers to act fairly in the execution of their powers to prevent, detect and solve crime."

On Wednesday, the woman told of her "overwhelming sense of shock, violation, anger and humiliation" as Street was sentenced.

The court also heard Street encouraged colleagues in WhatsApp messages to "bully" a teenage detainee.

News.title: British-American author and critic Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
News.content:
British-American author and cultural commentator Bonnie Greer has died at the age of 77 after a brief illness, her husband has said.

In a statement delivered with "profound sadness", Greer's widower David Hutchins noted how the acclaimed playwright and critic had made "an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life" with her "intelligence, courage and distinctive voice".

He added: "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her."

Hutchins continued: "Those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together."

The former boss of civil rights group Liberty has urged the government to consider banning the ‘Patriot Platform’ group behind anti-migrant protests that saw masked and hooded men descend on Dover and Portsmouth.

Shami Chakrabarti, who was Labour’s shadow attorney general between 2016 and 2020, hit out at the group she says “appears explicitly to intend and incite violence and intimidation”, and whose uniforms “signify a private army”.

Ms Chakrabarti was a high-profile critic of ministers' controversial decision to ban Palestine Action under terror legislation, which she suggested had led to the prosecution of many peaceful protesters.

But she said it was time to “at least give consideration” to proscribing Patriot Platform, or lawmakers risk losing the support of the public “over inaction in the face of rising threats, and perceived double standards”.

open image in gallery Masked men as part of the Dover protests ( PA )

Under the Terrorism Act 2000, the home secretary may proscribe an organisation if they believe it is concerned in terrorism, and it is proportionate to do so. Once an organisation is proscribed, it is illegal to join or support it.

The group, led by far-right activist Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, recently coordinated disruptive protests in Dover and Portsmouth, where masked supporters blocked roads and attempted to intercept newly arrived migrants.

Mr Thomas, a former bodyguard for Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson, established the anti-immigration movement after previously serving a prison sentence for attempted kidnapping.

On its website is the slogan: “Together, we will take our country back.”

Ms Chakrabarti, a Labour peer, will make the call as she gives the Lord Speaker’s Lecture this evening.

She will say: “To be clear, I have spoken against the blanket banning of face coverings at protests. We must protect the immune compromised and those who reasonably fear repercussions when protesting outside the embassy of a repressive state or office of an abusive employer.

“Nonetheless, political uniforms in public were understandably banned by section 1 of the Public Order Act 1936…

“I maintain my view that the proscription of Palestine Action was a disproportionate and counterproductive mistake, given the breadth of that movement and the possibility of prosecuting the violent few rather than the peaceful many. That issue is of course pending before the Supreme Court.

“Still, I wonder whether it isn’t time to at least give consideration to the proscription of the so-called Patriot Platform after recent events on our south coast. That is if we as legislators, are not to lose the public over inaction in the face of rising threats, and perceived double standards.”

open image in gallery Former Liberty director Shami Chakrabarti has made the call ( Getty )

She told The Independent that the distinction between Palestine Action and Patriot Platform is “not whether we agree with one or the other’s politics”.

“The former appears to have thousands of supporters interested in nothing but completely peaceful dissent and a few involved in criminal damage,” she explained. “The latter appears explicitly to intend and incite violence and intimidation and its uniforms signify a private army.”

She added: “It’s perhaps understandable that we choose to forget, but we have been here before in the 1930s with gangs of well-organised black-shirts inciting violence and seeking to intimidate.

“Freedom of expression and association is precious but not without limits. Surely, this is exactly the sort of case that proscription under the Terrorism Act was designed for?”

open image in gallery Ms Chakrabarti previously criticised the treatment of Palestine Action (Jonathan Brady/PA) ( PA Wire )

Her remarks come amid heightened tensions triggered by anti-migrant protests, counter-protests and and a series of online rumours that have divided communities across the UK.

Locals in Dover reported feeling unsafe in their own town earlier this month when a large group of “intimidating” masked demonstrators blocked roads and access to the port.

It comes after hundreds of protesters, dressed in black and wearing face coverings, blocked roads and were heard chanting “stop the boats”.

Traffic was stopped from going in and out, while government condemned “the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused”.

A group was later seen marching through the town chanting “whose streets? our streets!” and “stop the boats” as dozens of police officers followed.

The Home Office were approached but do not comment on specific organisations.

King Charles allegedly told Princess Diana’s brother to “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough” days after her tragic death, according to a bombshell new memoir set to be serialised in the Daily Mail.

Charles, who was prince at the time, made the apparent remarks to Earl Spencer during a major dispute over funeral arrangements after Diana died in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997.

The argument came after the decision was made to have princes William and Harry, who were aged 15 and 12 at the time, walk in their mother’s funeral procession, a decision that has since been the public of widespread public debate.

Earl Spencer claims, in his memoir titled Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, that he argued Diana would not have wanted her sons to join the procession.

open image in gallery (Left to right) Earl Spencer, Prince William, Prince Harry and King Charles III, the then Prince of Wales, waiting as the hearse carrying the coffin of Diana, Princess of Wales prepares to leave Westminster Abbey following her funeral service ( PA )

Charles afterwards phoned him, and remarked in a “stream of anger” that his ex-wife would soon be forgotten.

“He unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. ‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough!’” the memoir claims.

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson told The Sun: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

The Independent has contacted Buckingham Palace for comment. It has not seen Earl Spencer’s memoir detailing the allegations.

The book is likely to be highly critical of the royal family, and comes during a painful period marked by several scandals and family disputes.

open image in gallery Earl Spencer delivered a eulogy at Diana’s funeral in Westminster Abbey (John Stillwell/PA) ( PA Archive )

The Daily Mail says the book will include a “string of further extraordinary claims about Diana’s failed marriage to King Charles and the tumultuous aftermath of her tragic death in a car crash in Paris in 1997”.

It was reported earlier today that copies of Charles Spencer’s new memoir about his sister Princess Diana have been stolen from a lorry ahead of its release date, according to reports.

Diana’s death in 1997 caused an outpouring of grief across the world and especially in the UK, where she was a very popular figure.

open image in gallery King Charles visited the Cairngorms in Scotland on Wednesday, before the allegations came out ( Getty )

But her death exposed a rift between the royal family and the British public who were angry at the royals’ reserved response, which failed to match the grief of the rest of the nation.

Prince William and Prince Harry have spoken out about the day of their mother’s funeral.

The latter recently said while speaking to royal biographer Angela Levin for her book ‘Harry: Conversations with the Prince': “I don’t think any child should be asked to do that, under any circumstances. I don’t think it would happen today.”

“No child should lose their mother at such a young age and then have his grief observed by thousands of people.”

Prince William said in a 2017 BBC documentary called Diana 7 Days that he felt “completely numb, disorientated, dizzy”.

News.title: Death row inmate who murdered 3 people execution-style set for lethal injection
News.content:

A judge's late-night intervention has temporarily halted the execution of a man convicted of killing two real estate agents in Georgia as Texas prepares to carry out a separate lethal injection on Wednesday for a man convicted of a triple murder.

The execution in Texas would mark the state's fifth execution this year, whereas Georgia has not conducted any during the same period. Nationwide, Florida remains the most active jurisdiction, accounting for more than half of the 25 executions carried out across the U.S. so far this year.

In Georgia, 53-year-old Stacey Humphreys was sentenced to death for malice murder and other charges stemming from the 2003 slayings of 33-year-old Cyndi Williams and 21-year-old Lori Brown in an Atlanta suburb. He was originally set to be executed by lethal injection of pentobarbital at 7 p.m. EDT at the state prison in Jackson.

Meanwhile, in Texas, 40-year-old LeJames Norman faces execution at 6 p.m. CDT at the state penitentiary in Huntsville. Norman received the death penalty for the 2005 fatal shootings of Samuel Roberts, 24, Tiffani Peacock, 18, and Celso Lopez, 38, during a home invasion in search of drugs.

open image in gallery Two executions were scheduled for Wednesday but one has been halted by a judge, for now ( AP )

The stay of execution for Humphreys was issued late Tuesday after his legal team submitted a petition under a new Georgia statute. The law allows individuals who suffered past abuse to seek sentence reconsiderations if a link can be established between that abuse and their offenses.

State prosecutors are currently appealing the judge's order, a move that could allow the execution to go forward Wednesday night. Should an appellate court determine that Humphreys is ineligible for a sentence reduction hearing prior to the scheduled time, the judge indicated the stay could be vacated.

An attempted robbery turned deadly

Norman and an accomplice, Ker’Sean Ramey, targeted a residence in Edna—a rural community approximately 100 miles (160 kilometers) southwest of Houston—expecting to steal cocaine, according to court records. Finding no drugs, they shot the three occupants: Lopez was struck four times, including three shots to the back of the head; Peacock was shot twice in the head; and Roberts sustained five gunshot wounds to his head, neck, and chest.

Norman was apprehended five months later while attempting to re-enter the U.S. from Mexico. After he pleaded guilty to capital murder, a jury handed down the death sentence.

Ramey was likewise convicted and sentenced to death for his role in the killings, with his execution slated for next week.

Norman’s defense team has submitted a final petition for a stay of execution to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Real estate agents murdered

The murders committed by Humphreys took place on Nov. 3, 2003, at a model home sales office for a new subdivision in Powder Springs. Prosecutors showed that he forced Williams and Brown to undress and relinquish their bank account PINs before shooting them.

Humphreys withdrew over $3,000 using their cards, later telling investigators he needed cash to cover a high-interest payday loan for his truck.

Authorities identified a black Dodge Durango matching his vehicle at the crime scene. When officers attempted to question him at his Dunwoody home days later, he fled, prompting a high-speed pursuit that ended with his arrest in Wisconsin.

Defense attorneys have also raised physical concerns, noting that Humphreys weighs around 370 pounds (170 kilograms) and suffers from medical conditions causing him to feel as though he is choking when flat on his back. Prison officials agreed to elevate the gurney and place blankets behind his upper body to assist his breathing during the procedure.

Furthermore, his lawyers argue his sentence was corrupted by a juror who concealed biases and coerced others into voting for death. While lower courts dismissed these claims on procedural grounds, U.S. Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor and two colleagues argued last year that the allegations warranted full consideration.

Humphreys’ attorneys also challenged his clemency proceedings, which were conducted by a reduced four-member panel after one member was ordered to recuse herself over a prior conflict of interest with the local prosecutor’s office. The State Board of Pardons and Paroles ultimately denied clemency on Tuesday.

Donald Trump “directly” ordered his administration to “cover up” millions of documents stemming from investigations into Jeffrey Epstein, according to the president’s now-former ally Tucker Carlson.

The right-wing media commentator told Vanity Fair that he urged the president in the summer of 2025 to release all the documents connected to the wealthy and well-connected sex offender, who died in prison in 2019, but Trump was not convinced.

“My position from the beginning with Trump, I said it to Trump, was, ‘I don’t understand why you would ever keep any of this stuff secret.’ And I got like a bunch of different answers,” Carlson, a former Fox News star, told Vanity Fair’s Chris Whipple.

“I don’t feel any need to cover for Epstein. So I said, ‘You shouldn’t either.’ In the end, it came from Trump directly,” he added.

Pressed by Whipple on what exactly came “directly” from the president, Carlson replied: “The order to cover it up came from Trump.”

open image in gallery Donald Trump’s now-former ally Tucker Carlson claims the president ‘directly’ ordered his administration to prevent the release of the Epstein files before members of Congress forced the Justice Department to publish them ( AFP/Getty )

“I asked him why. And he gave me this long, very emotional explanation that this was all a plot against him, like Russiagate,” he said.

After a protracted political battle with members of Congress who drew up legislation to compel the Department of Justice to publish the files, Trump reluctantly agreed to sign the measure into law late last year, kicking off an ongoing legal and political battle for a fuller picture of Epstein’s influence and alleged connections to a wider group of powerful figures who abused women and girls.

The president’s name appears thousands of times within the millions of documents released by the Justice Department under the Epstein Files Transparency Act. Trump socialized with Epstein throughout the 1990s and 2000s, and Epstein who once described himself as the president’s “closest friend.”

Trump has not been accused of any criminal wrongdoing in connection with Epstein, and one’s appearance in the Epstein files does not suggest otherwise. The president has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein and insists he cut ties with the pedophile years before he was under investigation.

In response to questions about the president’s recollection of his conversation with Carlson about the Epstein files and whether Carlson was accurate, the White House directed The Independent to Trump’s lengthy Truth Social post from April that called him, among others, “stupid,” “NUT JOBS,” “TROUBLEMAKERS,” “Hand Flailing Fools” and “LOSERS.”

open image in gallery A sign showing a photo of President Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein is displayed by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer during a press conference to announce oversight efforts on the files of convicted sex offender Epstein on February 26, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Trump said Carlson “couldn’t even finish College” and was “a broken man when he got fired from Fox, and he’s never been the same — Perhaps he should see a good psychiatrist!”

“Just as President Trump has said, he’s been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told The Independent.

“And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House Oversight Committee’s subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein’s Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him,” she added.

In his profile of Vice President JD Vance, Whipple probes whether the second most powerful person in government is a craven political opportunist or a MAGA true believer eyeing the presidency.

Vance and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles appeared to agree that the Epstein files will remain a political liability in 2028 as the vice president looks to expand the “Trump coalition” by bringing in Republican voters who believe the administration failed them.

open image in gallery Carlson broke with Trump n the aftermath of the Iran war after campaigning with the president and JD Vance in 2024 ( Getty )

“The people inordinately interested in Epstein,” Wiles told Vanity Fair, “are the new members of the Trump coalition. It’s the Joe Rogan listeners. It’s the people that are sort of new to our world. It’s not the MAGA base.”

While the Trump administration has been eager to close the book on the Epstein case, bipartisan pressure to investigate people in his orbit — including the president — has only accelerated, with members of Congress issuing subpoenas for interviews with high-profile figures, former employees and administration officials.

The House Oversight Committee has also performed a series of interviews with survivors, whose testimony has led to criminal referrals to at least two people connected to Epstein.

Carlson, meanwhile, has publicly tried to distance himself from the president in the wake of the Iran war, which the former Fox News personality called a betrayal of the “America First” movement that Carlson championed.

He campaigned alongside Trump and urged him to select Vance as his running mate during the 2024 campaign, but he is now not “interested” in talking to the president at all and has suggested developing a viable third party to compete against Democrats and the GOP.

Active-duty U.S. service members have leaked photos to CBS News that depict damage to American military infrastructure in the Middle East during the Iran war.

The images, which are undated and were shared anonymously, appear to show the aftermath of missile and drone strikes on U.S. facilities in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.

The previously unseen images underscore the far-reaching impact of President Donald Trump’s war with Iran, now in its seven month with no clear end in sight.

“This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public,” one service member told CBS News. “We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face.”

One photo, from Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Al Kharj, Saudi Arabia, shows a four-engine Boeing aircraft with a large section of its fuselage and radar dome missing. Debris is scattered across the runway and sand. Earlier images of what appeared to be the same damaged plane had circulated on social media in March.

open image in gallery Active duty US service members leaked images to CBS News showing Iranian damage to US positions in the Middle East. Pictured: US Army Paratroopers fire an M777 howitzer during a field artillery exercise in the Middle East earlier this summer ( US Central Command )

Another image from the base — which houses thousands of U.S. military personnel — shows a building gutted by a strike, with sections of its roof and walls torn away.

Photos from Camp Buehring and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait show similar destruction: a charred truck, a damaged three-story building and a field of trailers flattened after a strike. Another image shows a dark plume of smoke rising from what appears to be a large tent-like structure.

The CBS News report quickly gained traction on social media, drawing more than 1 million views on X alone and prompting reactions from former U.S. military personnel and policy experts.

“This is shocking to me after having served at some of these locations,” wrote Fred Wellman, a retired Army officer and Democratic candidate for Congress in Missouri.

“The ‘damaged’ AWACS [Airborne Warning and Control System] has suffered a catastrophic hit,” wrote Sina Azodi, a professor of Middle East studies at George Washington University, referring to the image of the Boeing aircraft.

The Independent has contacted the Pentagon and White House for comment.

open image in gallery One of the installations that sustained damage was Camp Buehring in Kuwait. Pictured: US military personnel participate in the Best Squad Competition at the Buehring base camp in Kuwait on May 10, 2023 ( AFP via Getty Images )

Trump administration officials, who say the war is necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, have repeatedly emphasized the damage U.S. forces have inflicted on Iran.

They have said Iran’s military has effectively been wiped out and that vast numbers of Iranian leaders have been killed.

“Iran is officially a Failed Nation,” President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social last month. “They have no Navy, they have no Air Force, they have no currency, they are not paying their soldiers or police, Inflation is at 300%, and their leadership is in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country.”

At the same time, Trump and members of his administration have said little about damage the U.S. military has sustained and, at times, have appeared to minimize it.

In March, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth described Iranian strikes on U.S. bases as “squirters,” telling reporters that “every once in a while you might have one” that penetrates air defenses.

Last week, Trump denied reports that Iranian strikes had damaged U.S. military aircraft in Jordan. Asked by a NewsNation journalist whether there was truth to the report, Trump replied: “None whatsoever…No damage. No nothing.”

Yet, the U.S. has paid a heavy price for the war, measured in lives lost and economic ramifications.

Some 18 U.S. service members have been killed and more than 700 have been wounded, according to the Pentagon. In Iran, at least 3,636 people have been killed, according to HRANA, a U.S.-based human rights group.

open image in gallery ‘Iran is officially a Failed Nation,’ President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social last month. ‘IT IS DEAD!’ ( Reuters )

This week, the Pentagon’s inspector general acknowledged in a report that Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at American bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.

Last month, NBC News reported that Iran had inflicted “billions” of dollars in damage on U.S. intelligence infrastructure, including surveillance equipment, in the Middle East. That same month, CBS News reported that the U.S. military had used nearly all of its stockpiled long-range precision missiles during the conflict — an assessment Trump disputed.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimated this week the Iran war has cost the Pentagon about $38 billion, amounting to about $246 million per day. The broader U.S. economy has also been impacted, with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a major oil supply route, triggering spikes in global fuel prices. On Wednesday, the average price of a gallon of gasoline in the U.S. stood at $4.63, according to AAA, up from $2.98 two days before the war began.

Recent polling suggests the war is broadly unpopular in the U.S. A July AP-NORC survey found that just 28 percent of Americans approved of Trump’s handling of the conflict.

Amazon is raising starting wages for some workers and giving all U.S. employees new grocery discounts and access to a banking benefit.

Starting September 27, full-time U.S. employees in Amazon’s core operations roles will earn at least $20 an hour, a $1 increase, the company announced Wednesday. The roles include workers who pick, pack and sort customer orders, as well as those involved in transporting them. Many of the positions do not require prior experience.

The move brings average hourly pay for its U.S. core operations employees to nearly $24 an hour, Amazon says.

The increase comes as Amazon heads into the holiday shopping season, when the company typically adds workers to handle increased demand. Amazon said its minimum starting pay has increased by more than 17 percent over the past three years.

“We also have an annual step plan where pay increases the first three years someone is with us, providing a clear path for how their pay can grow over time,” Udit Madan, the senior vice president for Amazon’s worldwide operations, wrote in a blog post.

Amazon is raising the minimum starting pay for full-time operations workers to $20 an hour and introducing new grocery discounts and lifetime banking benefits for U.S. employees ( Reuters )

Additionally, starting October 1, every Amazon employee in the U.S. will also be eligible for new discounts on groceries and everyday essentials.

Employees will receive 10 percent off eligible fresh groceries and everyday essentials purchased through Amazon.com and Whole Foods Market Online. The discount is uncapped, according to Amazon.

Workers will also receive 20 percent off purchases at physical Whole Foods Market stores, including the retailer's hot bar and salad bar. The discount can be combined with existing Prime member discounts.

Amazon has expanded its grocery business in recent years, including through its ownership of Whole Foods Market, which it acquired in 2017. The company has also expanded same-day grocery delivery to more communities across the U.S.

Wednesday’s announcement also introduced a financial benefit called Day 1 Financial, through First Tech Federal Credit Union.

The program will give qualified employees and their spouses and children access to banking services that they can keep for life, even after leaving Amazon. The accounts will have no overdraft or monthly maintenance fees and no account minimums for standard checking and savings accounts. A credit history will not be required to open those accounts, Amazon said.

The benefit also includes access to thousands of surcharge-free ATMs, up to $300 a year in out-of-network ATM fee reimbursements, direct deposit, mobile and online banking and credit-building programs. Employees who qualify can also apply for credit cards and loans.

Amazon said the banking benefit will begin rolling out later in 2026 and become broadly available in 2027.

The new benefits build on Amazon's existing employee offerings, including free Prime memberships for eligible workers, health care starting at $5 a week with $5 copays under an eligible plan, prepaid education programs, a 401(k) with company matching and paid parental leave.

Amazon's latest pay increase follows a similar compensation investment announced by the company in September 2025, when it said average pay for fulfillment and transportation employees would rise above $23 an hour and average total compensation would exceed $30 an hour with benefits.

While American workers routinely face unpaid time off or a complete lack of paid family leave, Senator Mitch McConnell returned to Capitol Hill after a 92-day absence with a guaranteed paycheck.

The return of the 84-year-old Kentucky Republican — who missed three months following a fall — has sparked widespread online debate regarding taxpayer-funded salaries for absent lawmakers.

“POV ur returning after 3 months of paid leave and he@lthcare sponsored by the American people who don’t even have the same,” one widely circulated post on Instagram states.

The post quickly drew reactions highlighting the gap between congressional benefits and standard corporate or medical leave policies.

“Meanwhile my job decided that me being hospitalized for a prolonged miscarriage and multiple cyst ruptures at the same time wasn’t a ‘good enough’ reason for them to approve disability and I had to reimburse them for all of the money they paid me during that time,” one user commented. “I lost a baby and 3 weeks of pay. I love this country.”

open image in gallery Kentucky Senator Mitch McConnell returned to Capitol Hill Monday following a three-month absence after he was hospitalized for a fall and pneumonia this summer ( Getty )

Other internet commentary targeted the optics of the senator’s physical return to the chamber. Footage broadcast from Capitol Hill showed McConnell arriving in a wheelchair and speaking briefly with reporters before casting a procedural vote.

Reactions across X included satire and criticism regarding his appearance and responsiveness.

“Mitch looks like he is a zombie being remotely controlled,” one X user wrote. “This is SO STRANGE!!!! Is he even alive?”

“Mitch McConnell is the deadest alive person,” another X user chimed in.

That digital mockery extended beyond text posts. Instagram user dxfilms posted a carousel of bizarre, AI-generated images showing McConnell wearing sunglasses and a loud Hawaiian shirt, completely slumped over while Donald Trump and Marco Rubio pushed his wheelchair, held his hand or tried to prop him up during lunch.

Comedian and actress Aimee Lajoie also joined in, posting a video dressed as the senator with the caption, “Mitch McConnell on his way to sign your rights away.”

open image in gallery An AI-generated image posted by Instagram user dxfilms depicts McConnell wearing sunglasses and a Hawaiian shirt, accompanied by President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio ( dxfilms/Instagram )

Financial disclosures show that McConnell continued pulling in his standard annual salary of $174,000 throughout his recovery. He accumulated roughly $43,500 over the 92 days he was away from the Senate floor, as reported by The Daily Beast.

Public data additionally revealed that payroll for McConnell’s office ran uninterrupted during his leave. Figures from U.S. Census Bureau datasets indicated that six top staffers brought in a combined total of $318,688 while he was out, with total payroll for his entire office staff hitting about $893,872 during that period.

McConnell addressed reporters outside the Senate chamber on Monday, acknowledging the intense public speculation that mounted during his nearly three-month hiatus.

open image in gallery McConnell returned to Capitol Hill to cast a vote, as the chamber decided on a nomination to fill an opening on a district court bench in Ohio ( Reuters )

“I must admit, after two years of — two decades, actually — of dodging your questions, I wasn't sure how many of you would be here today,” McConnell said. “So I'm glad to see you. Time to get back to work, finish the job of this Congress.”

In a formal statement released Monday, McConnell called his recovery a “long and often frustrating process” complicated by the “lingering effects of childhood polio.”

He mentioned that while he was not yet back to full strength, he had assured Senate Majority Leader John Thune that he would try to show up for major legislative votes.

McConnell announced last year that he would not run for re-election and planned to leave the Senate when his term ended.

News.title: Spurs finally score... but still lose
News.content:
“But that is why we cannot say it does not work for anyone. There are players who play every three days with no issues. They are very robust, their performances do not change too much. There are other players where the risk is bigger and the performances are different. I have to learn who is ready to play games every three days and who needs a rest so their performance level is not affected. I thought I had it quite clear in my mind with some, but with others, it is new, even for them, because they have not played as many games. We are learning.”

Liverpool were knocked out in the fourth round of this competition last season, losing 3-0 at home against Crystal Palace. Joe Gomez returns to the squad for the hosts tonight after an injury early in pre-season but Giovanni Leoni, Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Federico Chiesa remain out.

Tottenham are still without a league win or goal this season. Their 0-0 draw at home against Everton Saturday means they sit just above the relegation zone. Tottenham overcame Charlton in the second round, convincingly winning 5-1 at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium last month.

“I think we are working well,” Tottenham boss Roberto De Zerbi said. “We played 30 minutes, 25 minutes very well [against Everton]. In that moment we could score two goals. Then we lost maybe the confidence because we did not score. For sure we have to improve. For sure I have big confidence in my players, they are very good players.

“We have to improve, yes. We can say the coach has responsibility if we do not score, yes, I accept, no problem. We did not win any game so far, yes. We are disappointed, sorry for that. But we have other positive things, like I said we did not [concede goals] in the last two games and the things we have to improve, we start our work. Nothing changed in my project and my idea.”

News.title: England cruise to victory led by ‘absolute freak’ Brook
News.content:
Whatever his returns, there has been an extra focus to Brook’s approach this summer, possibly because he has learnt from a grievous indiscretion in Wellington last winter. While others chase the Indian Premier League, he is totally committed to England, taking his break while that tournament is on and playing every match in all formats for his country.

Brook had come to the crease at the fall of the first wicket and, while it is early days, England appear to have added another arrow to their quiver. They handed a debut to opener Aneurin Donald, with his cap presented in the pre-match huddle by Pietersen, the new “specialist mentor”.

Donald has been selected as an “intent merchant”, charged with going extremely hard from the first over, aping Phil Salt, who is missing with a quad injury. He did what he was asked to do, smearing his first ball for two, then pulling six to leg and hammering four through the offside before the first over was out. Another big shot, off Wellalage, in the second saw him well caught in the deep, but 12 off five had kickstarted the innings.

News.title: Max Dowman-mania could make League Cup hottest ticket in town
News.content:
At this rate, Arsenal supporters will be looking forward to Carabao Cup matches as eagerly as any Premier League or Champions League game, simply because it will be a chance to watch Dowman again. The forward’s age and inexperience means he is still used sparingly in those high-priority competitions. The League Cup, by contrast, may prove to be his domain over the coming months.

Dowman’s double at Portman Road made him just the second 16-year-old to score two goals in a game for a Premier League side. The first was Wayne Rooney, for Everton against Wrexham in 2002.

The two goals underlined why there is so much excitement around Dowman. The first was a demonstration of his prodigious dribbling ability, as he weaved through Ipswich’s defence and buried his shot with the weaker right foot. The second showed his composure: a slotted finish, rolled in with ease.

News.title: UK borrowing costs hit 19-year high as global bond rout intensifies
News.content:
The cost of UK government borrowing hit its highest level since 2007 in a fresh global debt sell-off.

The yield on 10-year gilts, a benchmark for what the Treasury pays to borrow money, rose from 5.37pc to a fresh 19-year high of 5.41pc on Tuesday as rising oil prices risk reigniting inflation.

Mortgage experts have warned that residential and buy-to-let mortgage rates are set to climb towards 5pc, as market turmoil threatens to filter through to household finances.

Short-term debt costs have also jumped, with the yield on two-year UK bonds surpassing 4.9pc for the first time in three years.

The bond chaos came as Andy Haldane, a former Bank of England chief economist, warned that Labour risked becoming “just a traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok videos”.

He told LBC that John Healey’s original plan for a “low drama budget” had been “torpedoed” by higher borrowing costs and “events over the last couple of weeks”.

He said: “I think that [the bond market turmoil] will mean some hard choices next month at the Budget.”

“Few hard choices so far, but one is looming on the horizon, how any hole to the budget headroom is made good on. Is that a question of tax rises, or is it a question of taking the knife to public spending.”

Mr Haldane has been advising Labour since Andy Burnham took power.

It comes as the US Federal Reserve and the Bank of England face pressure to raise interest rates this week to combat rising prices.

Anthony Brinkman, a portfolio manager at Principal Asset Management, said: “The recent gilt market movements seem to be intent on showing central banks they are out of time – the market is expecting action.”

Borrowing costs around the world are rising after a 20pc surge in oil prices so far this month.

Brent crude tipped above $109 a barrel this week after Houthi rebels in Yemen, considered a proxy for Iran’s forces, seized control of a key port in the Red Sea, threatening shipping.

The US Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates on Wednesday in the face of the inflation threat.

As a result, the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds has surged above 5pc for the first time since 2007.

News.title: AI could transform global inequalities or ‘widen the gap’, warns Bill Gates
News.content:
“AI could be a great equaliser, or [it could] widen the gap”, says Mr Gates. “This is not a long-range prediction. It’s a present-tense choice”.

“We can harness AI for good. But it won’t happen by accident. After all, the market is an extraordinary engine of innovation, but a terrible guarantor of equal opportunity.

“With AI, the gap could grow even faster … That is what makes this moment so urgent. Things are changing rapidly, and the window to shape who benefits from AI, and how soon, is short”.

The key issue holding back the deployment of AI in the developing world revolves around the availability of local data and, in turn, the ability for the technology to scale in environments very different from where it is currently being created.

An app that is trained on billions of hours of American English, will struggle at first with British English (see your spell check) but is next to useless if your local language is Swahili or Chichewa.

More profoundly, an AI tool that allows a farmer in Hampshire to control his combine harvester remotely, will offer little to a smallholder in South Sudan who works the land by hand and faces a completely different array of pests, weather conditions and costs.

The same is true for health. “A community health worker in Rwanda examining a baby with a fever faces different questions than a clinician in a well-resourced hospital - and the AI supporting her needs to reflect that”, says Mr Gates.

He adds: “Most of the world is invisible to today’s AI models. These AI systems were trained primarily on what exists on the internet – and the internet reflects a deeply unequal world. More than 90 percent of the data used to train early, large language models came from English-language sources. The communities that stand the most to gain from AI are largely absent from the knowledge base these tools are built on. They are not just underserved. They are not in the picture at all”.

The new investment aims to help correct that. Mark Suzman, CEO of the Gates Foundation, says investments are already being made with companies including Microsoft and Google to build databases of a much wider range of languages, for instance.

Africa alone has more than 2,000 languages, and for AI’s to be effective there they have to understand what and how people actually speak - “their dialects, accents, and slang, too”.

The investments, he says, are being made on the condition that the intelligence and knowledge they accumulate are made freely available for others to use.

Languages for AI “are true public goods, almost definitional public goods. They need to be freely available to everybody. Once they’re created, they are public goods that can be uploaded onto any AI,” said Mr Suzman.

News.title: Reynolds refuses four times to rule out tax raid on state pensioners
News.content:
The Business Secretary refused four times to rule out retirees paying tax on the state pension from next year.

Jonathan Reynolds declined to reassure pensioners that they would not pay income tax on the benefit for the first time, saying it was a question for the Chancellor.

The comments on Tuesday raised concern for millions of retired people expecting to see their state pension surpass £13,000 from April, forcing them to pay income tax.

However, pensions minister Torsten Bell later insisted Labour would not put up taxes on people who rely on the state pension.

It is still unclear how this will be implemented given the complexity of separating the tax arrangements of different groups of pensioners.

The rise under the triple lock guarantee would drag many pensioners into paying income tax for the first time because their state income would surpass the personal allowance of £12,570.

Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, said last year that people solely reliant on the state pension would not have to pay the tax.

However, Mr Reynolds was repeatedly asked on BBC Breakfast whether Labour would honour this commitment after the next increase in the state pension in April. He declined to answer four times.

He said: “I’m sorry, that is for the Chancellor and for a Budget.

“The majority of pensioners in this country don’t just rely on the state pensions. Some do, I accept that, but the majority don’t.

“Sometimes when this is looked at, we’re focusing just on the state pension side of this. You’ve got to consider the full range of income retired people in the UK have.”

However Mr Bell, the pensions minister, walked back from Mr Reynolds comments.

He said: “In line with the commitment made at Budget 2025, pensioners who only just exceed the personal allowance will not have the administrative burden of paying small amounts of tax in this Parliament.

“The Chancellor will set out further details on how that commitment will be delivered at the Budget.”

Former pensions minister Sir Steve Webb said only one in 16 pensioners would benefit from this policy.

He said: “Those on the new state pension can expect to see an increase of nearly £500 per year next April.

“But the sting in the tail is that this will take the standard rate of the new state pension above the tax threshold.”

The comments came after official figures on Tuesday indicated the triple lock will rise by 3.9pc from April.

Under the triple lock, the state pension rises each April in line with inflation, average wages or 2.5pc, whichever is highest.

Total pay, including bonuses, rose by 3.9pc in the three months to July, down from 4.2pc in the three months to June.

Pensioners may yet receive a bigger increase if September’s inflation figure is higher than 3.9pc. That will be revealed next month but a higher figure is thought to be unlikely.

News.title: Outstanding Leeds cut short Jaissle’s Newcastle honeymoon
News.content:
The foundations are being put in around the stadium for a cavernous new West Stand, and Farke’s remit is to ensure that Leeds will be firmly established in the Premier League by the time it is completed in the summer of 2028.

To be fair to Farke, he has laid a sturdy base for this team to thrive and it felt before kick-off that this was going to be a big evening for Leeds, who had made a quietly encouraging start to the campaign and had negotiated three challenging away trips without defeat.

Big? It turned out to be spectacular. The first half was so one-sided that a boxing referee would not have allowed Newcastle to come out for the second, such was the pummelling they received; wave after wave of white-shirted raids left the visitors black and blue.

Aside from one little rick inside the opening 10 minutes, when James Trafford dithered and presented Yoane Wissa with a chance to mug him, Leeds were every bit as sensational as Newcastle were shocking, seizing on the opportunity to go on a rampage.

Leeds would have been in front after 11 minutes but Ethan Ampadu’s fierce drive battered into Calvert-Lewin’s legs and bounced away. Normally in such circumstances, players will wave an arm to berate their bad luck, but Ampadu, celebrating his 26th birthday, smiled: he, like everyone else, sensed what was coming.

Jayden Bogle, Justin and Nico Elvedi all had opportunities to open the scoring earlier, but eventually, they found the weak spot. Newcastle, who had lost the influential Nico González to a potential concussion, had replaced him with Sean Steur and what an influence he would have on matters.

On the half hour, Steur was a fraction too late getting out to close down Tanaka, whose shot ricocheted off him and to Lewis Miley, before looping away from Lukas Hornicek and dropping into the corner of the net in dam-busting fashion.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel can't watch Argentina collapse back - but now accepts blame for agonising exit
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel can't watch Argentina collapse back - but now accepts blame for agonising exit

England manager Thomas Tuchel initially blamed 'England's footballing DNA' for their heartbreaking World Cup defeat to Argentina - but now admits he made a big mistake

View 3 Images Thomas Tuchel admitted he went defensive too early during England's heartbreaking defeat to Argentina

Thomas Tuchel has revealed he has still not been able to watch back England’s World Cup semi final defeat as it was an “agony of epic proportions.”

‌



England boss Tuchel admitted he went defensive too early against Argentina because he felt his side were waiting for “death” with the game slipping away from them.

‌



Tuchel was talking on the FA’s Reflections show and said he could only bring himself to watch clips of the game with his other coaches at St George’s Park last week.

‌



But Tuchel admitted that he has not watched the game in its entirety and, while reviewing the Argentina heartbreak, repeated back some commentary which he says summed it up.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



Tuchel said: “Agony of epic proportions. I watched the clips with my coaches just last week when we were at SGP.

“My mind always works forward, forward. Painful. I see it now for the first time from the commentators’ point of view. It’s my scar, the players’ scar, I have to live with it. No-one is hurt more than me. It is torture.”

Tuchel said after the Argentina defeat that part of the problem was down to England’s DNA and a failure to keep the ball rather than negative tactics.

‌



But on reflection, Tuchel said that he got it wrong when he saw the game slipping away from England even before Anthony Gordon gave them the lead. Argentina’s late comeback knocked England out.

View 3 Images England suffered more World Cup agony after failing to hold on against their old rivals (Image: Getty)

Tuchel admitted they were outwitted and outsmarted by Argentina and their experience together with their tactics.

‌



Tuchel added: “We relied on our brotherhood, our mentality. Individual quality. Argentina have that as well - brotherhood, mentality, they bring it all to the table and it means the world to them.

“You have to have football quality. We prepared so well. I think we did quite well in the first half, it was quite an even match and I felt we were there.

“But from the start of the second half, I saw a change. The famous tackle of Djed Spence. And it did something to me, it did something to the players and it was a shift in the mindset. We played like we had four minutes left but there was half an hour left.

‌



View 3 Images Tuchel claims the brilliant tackle by Djed Spence changed his and the England players' mindsets

“Argentina played very, very quickly. They had nothing to lose. We conceded a chance just before the water break. I thought we will not survive. This is death.

“I thought: ‘OK, let’s change to a back five, a 5-4-1.’ It was too early for that mindset. It was Congo, Miami and Norway and then Mexico and altitude. We were super tired.”

Article continues below

Tuchel says, however, beating France to finish third does count. “You learn as a coach. You have to play as if it is 0-0. That includes me as well,” he said.

“I have a lot of people who want to see my medal. We did not achieve what we wanted. But I am still very proud of what we achieved. These players will come back hungry.”
