The guidance says previous Argentine measures did not prevent the islands' economy from growing, without specifying which. In 2012, Argentina barred Borders and Southern Petroleum, Desire Petroleum, Argos Resources and Falkland Oil and Gas for twenty years. In 2015, a prosecutor ordered the seizure of more than US$156 million in international equipment, including vessels, platforms and bank accounts.

The islands' Legislative Assembly welcomed the publication in a statement that largely reproduces the guidance's own wording. Argentina claims sovereignty over the islands; in the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: Milei prepares bill to toughen sanctions on companies operating in the Falklands
World.content:
Milei prepares bill to toughen sanctions on companies operating in the Falklands

15th Tuesday, September 2026 - 09:53 UTC Full article

The package will be a legislative test for Milei, whose libertarian coalition lacks majorities in Congress

Argentine President Javier Milei is preparing legislation this week to toughen sanctions against companies operating in the Falklands, a move analysts say could raise tensions with Britain beyond the oil sector.

The bill, titled the National Sovereignty Defense Law, would amend Law 26,659, which already bars unauthorized hydrocarbon activity on the disputed continental shelf and provides for disqualifications of between five and twenty years. Milei announced it on September 3 in a televised address, alongside a decree to speed up existing sanctions proceedings. The text will be introduced in the lower house.

The legislation builds on proceedings the Argentine government says it has opened against at least 60 companies and individuals linked to offshore oil exploration around the archipelago, which Argentina calls the Malvinas and claims as its own despite British control. Argentina invaded the Islands in 1982 and fought a ten-week war before surrendering to Britain. Islanders confirmed their status as a British Overseas Territory in the 2013 referendum.

Congressional aide Marcelo Seghini told Reuters the text provides for tougher penalties for unauthorized operations and would extend sanctions to affiliates and to other activities affecting Argentine natural resources. According to the same source, the government is considering including the fishing industry, which underpins much of the Islands' economy. The Argentine government has not confirmed that scope or responded to queries about the companies affected.

The move follows a criminal complaint filed last week against companies linked to the offshore Sea Lion project, operated by Israel's Navitas Petroleum alongside Britain's Rockhopper Exploration. Both maintain the project holds valid licenses from the Falklands government and do not expect Milei's actions to derail development.

A government document reviewed by Reuters lists shareholders and financial intermediaries among the firms marked for possible sanctions, including Vanguard, First Eagle, Canaccord, Interactive Investor and Hargreaves Lansdown. Oilfield services providers SLB, Baker Hughes and Halliburton have said in recent days they will not take part in activities on the Islands.

The announcement followed comments by U.S. President Donald Trump suggesting Washington could reconsider its neutral position on the dispute. For Marcelo Elizondo, Argentina's representative to the International Chamber of Commerce, this was not a bill prepared over time: Trump's remarks, he said, “created a climate that the government sought to exploit quickly.”

The package will be a legislative test for Milei, whose libertarian coalition lacks majorities in Congress. Opposition lawmaker Aldo Leiva said the president “is clearly using the Malvinas for political opportunism.”

Companies and investors are weighing whether the sanctions could ultimately reach firms with operations in Argentina, including the Vaca Muerta shale formation. Congress receives the 2027 budget proposal on Tuesday, with defense spending expected to rise.

World.title: In Grito, President Sheinbaum celebrates migrants, women insurgents and the dignity of Mexico’s diverse peoples
World.content:
Listen to this article

From the central balcony of the National Palace and in front of a huge crowd of celebrants gathered in Mexico City’s central square, President Claudia Sheinbaum delivered the national Cry of Independence (Grito de Independencia) on Tuesday night, the eve of Mexico’s Independence Day.

“Mexicanas, Mexicanos, long live independence!” Sheinbaum declared 216 years after priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla issued the Cry of Dolores (Grito de Dolores) — a call for revolt against Spanish rule.

En el 216 Aniversario del Grito de Independencia, exaltamos a los héroes y heroínas que nos dieron patria, como Antonia Nava. También destacamos a los pueblos indígenas y afromexicanos, así como a nuestros hermanos y hermanas migrantes. ¡Que viva México libre, independiente y… pic.twitter.com/bJXNXaB43m — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) September 16, 2026

With the presidential sash draped over her torso, the Mexican flag in her left hand and her husband, Jesús María Tarriba, standing beside her, Sheinbaum issued a total of 21 arengas, or “cries of viva!“, each of which was met with a reciprocal “¡viva!” by those present in the Zócalo and Mexicans across the country.

A selection of Mexico’s independence heroines and heroes, the nation’s Indigenous and Afro-Mexican people and Mexicans living abroad were all wished long life by Sheinbaum, who made history a year ago by becoming the first female president of Mexico to deliver the Grito. In a year in which she has denounced U.S. interference in Mexican affairs, the president also issued an emphatic cry of ¡viva! in defense of Mexican independence and sovereignty.

“Long live Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla! Long live Josefa Ortiz Téllez-Girón! Long live José María Morelos y Pavón! Long live Leona Vicario! Long live Vicente Guerrero! Long live Gertrudis Bocanegra! Long live Guadalupe Victoria! Long live Antonia Nava!” Sheinbaum proclaimed.

“Long live the heroines and heroes who gave us a homeland! Long live the Indigenous and Afro-Mexican peoples! Long live our migrant sisters and brothers! Long live the dignity of the people of Mexico! Long live freedom! Long live equality! Long live justice! Long live democracy! Long live a free, independent and sovereign Mexico! ¡Viva México!”

Some of the people honored by the president, including Afro-Mexicans and the insurgent Antonia Nava, had never before been included in a national Cry of Independence.

After completing her second Grito, Sheinbaum rang the Campana de Dolores — the same bell that Hidalgo rang 216 years ago in the town of Dolores, Guanajuato — and waved the Mexican flag to the mass of people gathered in the Zócalo. The president received the flag from an escolta (color guard) made of up of six female military cadets.

After the Grito, a fireworks display lit up the sky above the Zócalo, where musical acts including the Grammy Award-winning Texan band Intocable played on Tuesday night.

Among the officials who witnessed Sheinbaum’s second Cry of Independence from National Palace vantage points were Attorney General Ernestina Godoy, Supreme Court Chief Justice Hugo Aguilar, Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez, Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard, Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla, Navy Minister Raymundo Pedro Morales and Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada.

Governors and mayors also issued Cries of Independence at ceremonies held on Tuesday night in cities and towns across the country.

No incidents reported at Mexico City’s 300,000-strong Independence celebration

The Mexico City government said in a statement that more than 300,000 people attended the Mexican Independence celebration in the Zócalo.

“The event took place peacefully and concluded without any casualties or incidents,” the government said.

“… Coordination between various agencies and the responsible participation of citizens allowed this commemoration to take place in an organized manner and in an environment of harmony,” the government said.

“The event also reflected the support of thousands of people for President Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, who went to the Zócalo to participate in a day of profound significance for the history and identity of the country, as well as to hear a message to the nation in defense of our independence, dignity, and sovereignty.”

With reports from Reforma and La Jornada

World.title: Is Mexico’s soccer league a monopoly? Antitrust officials are looking to find out
World.content:
The National Antitrust Commission (CNA) has unilaterally opened an investigation into Liga MX, Mexico’s top professional soccer league and a massive cultural touchstone that captures the country’s passion for the sport.

An internal CNA document says the investigation aims to identify “the possible commission of relative monopolistic practices in the market of ‘affiliation, organization and access’ to professional federated football competitions in Mexico, as well as similar or related services.”

⚽ ¿Cómo investigamos el funcionamiento de un mercado?

José Manuel Haro Zepeda, titular de nuestra Autoridad Investigadora, explicó en @MVSNoticias las herramientas con las que contamos para analizar la organización y acceso a competiciones de fútbol profesional en México. pic.twitter.com/r2qgofrR9M — Comisión Nacional Antimonopolio (@AntimonopolioMX) September 15, 2026

In short, the CNA wants to know if a small group is violating the Federal Law of Economic Competition by unfairly controlling who can join, who can compete and how tournaments are organized, to the exclusion of other interested parties.

“After analyzing the events that occurred in recent months, the Investigating Authority determined that it has sufficient evidence to formally open an investigation on its own initiative for possible monopolistic practices in the professional soccer market in Mexico,” the CNA said in a public report.

The recent events referred to are likely related to a Liga MX decision in July to scrap promotion/relegation between the top-flight Mexican soccer league and the second-tier Liga Expansión. Liga MX also announced the end to payouts to the second-tier sides.

Promotion and relegation were scrapped in 2020 to insulate the clubs from the financial impacts of lost revenue during the enforced lockdown ordered due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

Liga Expansión officials fiercely disputed the decision, even filing a suit with the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which ruled that the 2026-27 campaign was the earliest point at which promotion/relegation ought to be reinstituted.

Critics have also identified the league’s policy regarding possession of television broadcasting rights by teams as a monopolistic practice.

The commission has sought to make clear that there are no defendants identified as yet and it hasn’t been determined exactly who will be investigated. Instead, the probe will simply review whether competition law is being followed.

The investigation can last up to 120 business days, but can be extended up to three times longer if necessary. During that time, the CNA can request documents, visit offices, summon people to testify and conduct inspections.

If guilt is determined, the Liga MX and its member teams could face a penalty of up to 10% of their annual income and would be required to correct any monopolistic practices detected.

With reports from ESPN, El Economista, El Universal and SportCa

World.title: Should you be worried about the presence of brain-eating amoeba in Yucatán water bodies?
World.content:
A man died of Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM) in a Mérida hospital last week, most likely from contact with the brain-eating amoeba Naegleria fowleri, the Yucatán Health Services (SSY) reported on Monday.

The SSY confirmed the presence of N. fowleri in an artificial lake at the La Isla shopping center in Mérida, where the 34-year-old man worked as a water sports instructor.

FAMILIARES DESPIDEN A CARLOS, INSTRUCTOR QUE F4LL3C10 POR AMEBA COME CEREBROS#Video | Familiares y amigos despidieron con tristeza a Carlos, el joven instructor de wakeboard de 33 años que perdió la v1d4 tras contraer una agresiva infección por la ameba ‘Naegleria fowleri’ en… pic.twitter.com/f57zIqs8Ly — Yucatán Ahora (@yucatanahora) September 15, 2026

“It is a serious and extremely rare disease; this is the first case registered in Yucatán,” the SSY said in a statement.

The microorganism is most commonly found in stagnant, warm waters between 35°C and 46°C. It enters the body when contaminated water is forcefully inhaled through the nose, although it can also occur while swimming, diving or submerging one’s head in lakes, rivers or poorly chlorinated swimming pools.

PAM is not transmitted from person to person and is not acquired by drinking contaminated water, the SSY emphasized.

People living in the Yucatán capital have expressed concern about the water quality in nearby cenotes, where swimming is common. However, experts suggest that natural freshwater bodies are cooler, at between 24°C and 26°C, making the presence of N. fowleri far less likely.

The development of microorganisms in pools can be avoided through chlorination and pH management, and in larger water bodies through adequate water movement, which promotes aeration. Regular cleaning and maintenance can also help avoid the accumulation of sediment, organic matter, algae and biofilms in stagnant water, conditions that attract N. fowleri.

The first symptoms of PAM are usually severe headache, fever, nausea and vomiting. According to initial reports, the victim presented with severe symptoms of central nervous system infection and was taken to a hospital in the city, where he died.

Health authorities ordered the temporary closure of the water feature at La Isla while samples were tested at the Hidalgo State Public Health Laboratory, which confirmed the presence of N. fowleri. Meanwhile, cleaning efforts and technical inspections were carried out at the site.

Epidemiological investigators are conducting interviews to locate other individuals who may have come into contact with the water.

The SSY said it plans to investigate the companies responsible for water quality and lake maintenance for their compliance with Mexican rules and regulations.

“Anyone who has violated health regulations will be sanctioned,” the SSY stressed.

According to the SSY statement, once the responsible company demonstrates through laboratory tests that the lake water is suitable for recreational use in accordance with legal standards, a new verification and sampling of the water will be conducted and a decision will be made on whether to lift the temporary closure.

With reports from Reportur, La Jornada and Diario de Yucatán

World.title: 139 US troops cleared to enter Mexico for joint training in Chihuahua
World.content:
More than 100 U.S. soldiers will travel to Mexico this month to participate in joint training exercises with Mexican military personnel in the northern state of Chihuahua.

The federal Senate on Monday granted President Claudia Sheinbaum the authority to allow the entry into Mexico of 139 U.S. Army troops, who are scheduled to land at the Santa Gertrudis Air Force Base south of Chihuahua city this Sunday.

The granting of that authority comes amid security-related tension in the Mexico-U.S. relationship.

Among the causes of that tension are the CIA’s alleged participation in a drug lab raid in Chihuahua in April without the knowledge or authorization of the Mexican government; U.S. prosecutors’ drug-trafficking accusations against Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya and other current and former officials; and suggestions from Trump administration officials that the U.S. could take unilateral action against Mexican drug cartels on Mexican soil.

While each of those developments has drawn the ire of Sheinbaum, the president remains committed to cooperating with the Trump administration on security on the proviso that Mexican sovereignty and territorial integrity are respected. One example of that cooperation is a joint anti-drone operation that is currently taking place on the border between Tijuana and San Diego.

U.S. soldiers have previously traveled to Mexico to undertake joint training exercises with Mexican personnel. However, the U.S. contingent set to arrive in Chihuahua on Sunday is larger than previous ones that have come to Mexico.

Here’s everything you need to know about the upcoming military collaboration on Mexican soil.

Where will the joint training exercises take place?

The joint training exercises will take place at the Centro Nacional de Adiestramiento (National Training Center), located in Santa Gertrudis in the municipality of Saucillo, Chihuahua. The CNA is the Mexican military’s largest training facility.

Among the simulated combat exercises U.S. and Mexican military personnel will conduct are the destruction of sniper positions; the seizure of an airfield; an air assault; the destruction of a fuel-supply point; and the capture and extraction of a target using live fire.

The U.S. soldiers will stay at the CNA during their time in Mexico.

What is the objective of the training exercises?

The Senate said in a statement that the aim of the joint training exercises is to “strengthen operational capabilities between the United States and Mexican Armed Forces through the planning and execution of military operations under the principles of respect, sovereignty and territorial integrity; shared responsibility; mutual trust; and collaboration without subordination.

The Senate said that the joint training “will not only have a positive impact on strengthening individual and collective preparedness, but will also contribute to the improvement of bilateral military cooperation mechanisms.”

How long will the US soldiers remain in Mexico?

The U.S. troops will arrive in Chihuahua on a U.S. Air Force plane on Sept. 20 and return to the United States on Sept. 30. Therefore, the soldiers will be in Mexico for a total of 11 days.

The Senate noted that the U.S. troops will enter Mexico “with weapons.”

Which division of the US army to the soldiers belong to?

The 139 soldiers coming to Mexico belong to the 101st Airborne Division of the U.S. Army. The division, known as the “Screaming Eagles,” is the only air assault division of the United States Army. It is based at Fort Campbell, Kentucky.

With reports from La Silla Rota, El Economista and El Financiero

World.title: Tehran’s Azadi Tower bears Mexican flag in first-ever Independence Day tribute
World.content:
For the first time, Iran lit one of its most recognizable landmarks in the green, white and red of the Mexican flag, turning Tehran’s Azadi Tower into a striking Independence Day tribute Tuesday night.

The Azadi Tower illumination marked the 216th anniversary of the Grito de Dolores — the 1810 call by priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla that launched Mexico’s war for independence from Spain.

La emblemática Torre Azadi, símbolo de Teherán, se iluminó con los colores de la bandera mexicana para conmemorar el 216° aniversario de la Independencia de México. La Embajada de Irán en México destacó el acto como un gesto de amistad entre ambos pueblos. Más en La Jornada:… pic.twitter.com/tfgRRj5ddy — La Jornada (@lajornadaonline) September 15, 2026

“Today, Mexico is not in Mexico. It is in the heart of Iran,” the Iranian Embassy in Mexico posted Sept. 15 with a video of the glowing monument.

The display marked the first time Iran has illuminated a monument in honor of Mexico, according to the newspaper El Universal.

Those colors, however, are not inherently unusual at Azadi Tower, since green, white and red are also Iran’s national colors. For example, on Feb. 10, 2024, it was lit up in that way for the 45th anniversary of the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Speaking to HispanTV from Tehran, Mexican Ambassador Guillermo Puente Ordorica called the lighting “a great gesture of friendship” that Mexicans will cherish.

Built in 1971, the 45-meter Azadi Tower was originally called Shahyad Tower, then renamed Azadi (Persian for “freedom”) after the 1979 revolution. The tower and its surrounding square are often the site of major public gatherings.

Beyond Iran, Mexican communities and diplomats marked Día de la Independencia across several continents.

In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani was grand marshal Sunday at a Mexican Independence Day parade in Brooklyn, wearing a tricolor sash and carrying a Mexican flag. He said he was proud to be the first New York City mayor to march in the parade with “a community that has fostered cultural pride for generations.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani (@nycmayor)

Mamdani’s remarks came just days after U.S. Vice President JD Vance criticized a protester carrying a Mexican flag at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, calling him an “idiot” and telling him, “If you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket.”

Elsewhere, Mexico’s ambassador to the United Kingdom, Alejandro Gertz Manero, led a Grito ceremony in London, where festivities included music, food, dance and other traditions.

In Madrid, the Mexican Embassy hosted a public Grito in Chamberí Square, followed by folk ballet, mariachi and a circus performance.

Mexican celebrations were also reported in Krakow, Rome, Vienna, Beijing, Seoul, Barcelona, Budapest and Kansas City.

With reports from El Universal, La Jornada and Madrid Gazette

World.title: New US-Mexico water agreement means reduced allotments but a heathier Colorado River
World.content:
A long-running dispute between Mexico and the United States over Colorado River water-sharing has been resolved — at least for the next two years — with Mexico getting significantly less water as a result.

The U.S. is also receiving less water as part of a joint effort to mitigate ongoing drought conditions and low reservoir levels in the Colorado River basin.

In fact, under the new agreement, formally called Minute 334 and finalized by the International Boundary and Water Commission (IBWC) on Sept. 2, Mexico’s 16.7% (250,000 acre-feet) annual reduction of its previous typical water allocation is equivalent to water-use reductions imposed on U.S. Lower Basin states (Arizona, California and Nevada).

The agreement also implements a strategy to manage the salinity of Colorado River water as it reaches Mexico. Consultations regarding possible further cuts are contemplated for 2028 if conditions worsen.

Minute 334 was signed by Mexican IBWC Commissioner Adriana Reséndez and her U.S. counterpart, Chad McIntosh, with the participation of Mexican IBWC Secretary Manuel Morales. The U.S. Department of the Interior confirmed the approval of both governments.

“This Minute makes sure water is shared fairly among our users and protects the health of the Colorado River during these difficult times,” McIntosh said in a news release. “Both countries deserve a lot of credit for agreeing to these water reductions and other measures.”

Reséndez insisted on proportionality between the two countries, defending Mexico’s position even as it has struggled to meet its obligations in the original 1944 treaty.

When the most recent five-year cycle of that treaty came to an end on Oct. 24 last year, Mexico still owed 865,136 acre-feet of water, though the terms of the treaty grant Mexico five years to catch up.

The reduction agreed to in Minute 334 is equivalent to one-sixth of Mexico’s annual allocation established in the treaty, about 1.85 billion cubic meters.

The two nations also agreed to cooperate on managing the Colorado River Delta in Mexico, which has been transformed from a lush 2-million-acre wetland into a mostly dry salt flat due to decades of intensive upstream dam construction and water diversions.

With reports from El Universal, WaterWorld and The Colorado Sun

World.title: MND Local: WTA Tennis, an international film fest and more events in Guadalajara
World.content:
Late September in Guadalajara brings an action-packed calendar. Upcoming events include a World Migrant Day celebration benefiting a local nonprofit organization, an international film festival and the 2026 Guadalajara Open, an important stop on the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) professional tour.

Top female tennis players to compete at the Guadalajara Open this week

Following hard on the heels of the U.S. Open in New York City, Zapopan welcomes a select group of the WTA’s brightest stars to the Guadalajara Open this week.

The annual event, played at the Panamerican Tennis Center in Parque Metropolitano, attracts a diverse group of top female tennis players from around the globe. The field will compete in singles and doubles for a US $1.2 million purse and a top singles prize of US $185,500.

Confirmed players for this year’s event include world number 11 Marta Kostyuk of Ukraine and world number 14 and defending champion Iva Jovic of the United States.

Kostyuk returns to Mexico as one of the hottest players on the WTA tour during the 2026 season, having reached the semifinals of Wimbledon and Roland Garros, in addition to claiming two titles on clay last spring. She last competed at the Guadalajara Open in 2023, where she reached the second round.

Latin American tennis will also be well represented, with Colombian veteran Camila Osorio and Mexican No. 1 Renata Zarazúa scheduled to compete.

For details, visit the tournament website.

Dates: Sept. 13-19, 2026.

Sept. 13-19, 2026. Location: Centro Panamericano de Tenis, Zapopan, Jalisco.

Centro Panamericano de Tenis, Zapopan, Jalisco. Cost: Individual tickets start at 866 pesos, not including fees. Tournament packages are available on Boletomovil.

Aeroméxico to launch nonstop service from Guadalajara to Paris in 2027

Savoring the perfect pain au chocolat is about to get a little easier for Francophile Tapatíos. Starting April 13, 2027, the city will have its second direct European flight route, as Aeroméxico launches nonstop service between Guadalajara’s Miguel Hidalgo International Airport (GDL) and Paris-Charles de Gaulle (CDG).

The route will run three times per week on Tuesdays, Fridays and Sundays, departing Guadalajara at 1:55 p.m. and arriving in Paris at 9:25 a.m. the following day. Return flights will operate on Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays, departing Paris at 11:40 a.m. and arriving in Guadalajara at 4:10 p.m. the same day.

“Adding Guadalajara–Paris … strengthens our network, offers customers more travel options and further consolidates our position as the leading airline between Mexico and Europe,” Giancarlo Mulinelli, senior vice president of global sales at Aeroméxico, told Aviacionline last week.

Celebrate World Migrant Day with the Rhizome Center

Later this month, Guadalajara residents will have the opportunity to celebrate World Migrant Day at a community celebration featuring local food, culture and a social cause.

Hosted by The Rhizome Center, this year’s festival, “Many Journeys. One Community,” is both a fundraiser and an opportunity to raise awareness about the organization’s work. During the event, guests can sample food from 15 migrant kitchens, enjoy live French, Cuban and Syrian music, listen to storytelling, and meet artists sharing their craft and culture.

The Rhizome Center was founded in 2018 during President Donald Trump’s first term, with a mission to provide direct support to deportees and refugees sent to Mexico.

Since his return to office, the need has grown. Many deportees arrive with no resources or documentation to regularize their status in Mexico. Filling that void, the organization provides legal aid, crisis assistance, counseling and other services.

Run by executive director and founder Tran Dang, The Rhizome Center derived its name from plant rhizomes — the underground roots that provide essential nutrients — symbolizing humanity’s resilience and interconnectedness across borders.

For more information about The Rhizome Center for Migrants and details on how to support the cause, visit the group’s Instagram account. Donations are accepted via PayPal and Zelle.

Date: Saturday, Sept. 27, from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m.

Saturday, Sept. 27, from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. Location: Casa Zuno, Avenida Unión 2226, Colonia Americana, Guadalajara.

Casa Zuno, Avenida Unión 2226, Colonia Americana, Guadalajara. Cost: General admission is 375 pesos. VIP tickets are 500 pesos per person and guarantee a seat.

The MUBI film fest lands in Guadalajara next weekend

View this post on Instagram A post shared by MUBI México (@mubimexico)

Global distributor, producer and streaming service MUBI recently added film festivals to its portfolio and announced a Guadalajara edition from Sept. 18-20. The festival will screen independent feature films and shorts, alongside filmmaker Q&As, workshops, installations and DJ sets.

Anticipated films on the schedule include:

“Her Private Hell” by Nicolas Winding Refn

“Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?” by Garth Jennings

“Hope: The First Impact” by Na Hong-jin

“Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” by Jane Schoenbrun

“Rose” by Markus Schleinzer

For moviegoers seeking nostalgia, Ridley Scott’s 1991 feminist classic “Thelma & Louise,” starring Susan Sarandon, Geena Davis and Brad Pitt, is also on the schedule.

For full program details, visit Mubi Mexico’s website. In addition to Guadalajara, MUBI Fest 2026 made stops in Mexico City, São Paulo, Bogotá and Buenos Aires this year.

Dates: Sept. 18-20.

Sept. 18-20. Location: FICG Cineteca, Av. Perif. Pte. Manuel Gómez Morin 1695, Rinconada de la Azalea, Belenes Norte, Zapopan.

FICG Cineteca, Av. Perif. Pte. Manuel Gómez Morin 1695, Rinconada de la Azalea, Belenes Norte, Zapopan. Cost: Tickets available on the MUBI website.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Mexico City-area airports to halt takeoffs and landings for 4 hours tomorrow
World.content:
Takeoffs and landings at the Mexico City International Airport (AICM) will be suspended for four hours on Wednesday, Sept. 16, to ensure that military aircraft can operate safely in the capital’s airspace while the annual Independence Day parade takes place below.

The Mexican Navy, which operates the AICM, announced the suspension in a statement.

El AICM suspenderá operaciones aéreas por desfile del 16 de septiembre. ➡️ https://t.co/T6iEPTFtOa @aeropuertos_GAM pic.twitter.com/wJK8Khf3YB — Aeropuerto Internacional Benito Juárez CDMX (@AICM_mx) September 14, 2026

“To ensure the safety of the military air maneuvers that will be carried out to commemorate the 216th anniversary of the start of Mexico’s independence, and as directed by the aviation authority, the Mexico City Benito Juárez International Airport (AICM) will suspend aircraft takeoffs and landings on September 16 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.,” the navy said.

“According to NOTAMs [Notices to Airmen] A8260/26 and B1724/26, … issued by the Federal Civil Aviation Agency (AFAC) and disseminated through the Mexican Airspace Navigation Services (SENEAM), the airport will be closed to all types of flights during the specified hours.”

The Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA) in México state will also suspend takeoffs and landings between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. Wednesday. Military aircraft that will conduct flyovers as part of the Independence Day festivities will take off from the Santa Lucía Air Force Base, which adjoins AIFA.

The navy advised air passengers who have a flight scheduled for Wednesday to ask their airlines about the status of their flights as “this event will result in some adjustments to scheduled times.”

The Independence Day parade is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. Wednesday with a flyover of nearly 100 Air Force and National Guard airplanes and helicopters above the Zócalo, Mexico City’s central square — including F-5 fighters performing a fleur-de-lis maneuver.

The ground procession will start near the Zócalo, pass the Palacio de Bellas Artes (Palace of Fine Arts), continue along Juárez Avenue and Paseo de la Reforma, and end at the Campo Marte military complex near Chapultepec Park.

Mexico News Daily

It carries the editor’s leader, the full deep dive on the Federal Reserve’s decision and three ways the next six months can run, the country health check and the people who matter. Open the dossier · Browse the archive

Washington raised the price of money at two o’clock, and pointed higher for the year. The continent’s other capitals had arranged their afternoon around that hour.

Strasbourg did not wait. Europe offered Canada a place inside its own house, and nobody has yet written what the place would be in law.

Read across the Federal Reserve’s own statement, implementation note and projections, and across Treasury and Bank of Canada data. Then the Prime Minister’s Office, the European Commission, court and Justice Department filings, and our own Washington, Ottawa and Toronto desks.

The Committee Raises, And Points Higher

The Federal Open Market Committee raised its target range for the federal funds rate by a quarter point on 16 September 2026. The new range is 3.75 to 4.00 per cent, the committee’s own statement says.

That statement was released at 2 p.m. New York time. It says the committee “approved the following statement for release by a 12 – 0 vote”.

The desk read that release and found no named voting list on it. A tally without names is a committee speaking in one voice.

The range had stood at 3.50 to 3.75 per cent since the committee lowered it on 10 December 2025. Its five statements of 2026 before today each said maintain.

The statement gives its reason in one sentence: “Inflation remains elevated.” It adds that “Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal”.

On the economy it says activity “is expanding at a solid pace” and that “domestic spending has been resilient”. It also says: “Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.”

Before the decision, Reuters reported on 16 September that market pricing put the chance of a rise above 90 per cent. Kiplinger reported the CME FedWatch measure at 92.7 per cent for a quarter-point rise, read on 15 September.

Kiplinger’s 15 September entry called that measure a rate cut, while its own entry of 14 September called it a raise. The Federal Reserve’s own release has settled the direction.

The price was a wager, and the wager came in.

The projections matter more than the quarter point. Chairman Kevin Warsh has criticised such projections in public, and has now published his own.

The Summary of Economic Projections landed with the statement at 2 p.m. New York time. It puts the median federal funds rate at 4.1 per cent for the end of 2026.

The June projection put that median at 3.8 per cent. The new table puts 4.1 per cent for the end of 2027 and 3.9 per cent for the end of 2028.

June put those two at 3.6 and 3.4 per cent. A median of 4.1 per cent sits above the top of today’s range.

The desk reads that as one further quarter point before the end of 2026. The committee has published a path, not a promise.

The same table puts median inflation on the personal consumption expenditures measure at 3.7 per cent for 2026. June put that at 3.6 per cent.

It puts 2.3 per cent for 2027 and 2.1 per cent for 2028. The median unemployment rate is 4.1 per cent for each of 2026, 2027 and 2028.

June put the 2026 unemployment median at 4.3 per cent. The committee has revised its labour market view tighter rather than looser.

The implementation note sets the rates the decision runs on. Interest on reserve balances moves to 3.90 per cent and the primary credit rate to 4.00 per cent, both effective 17 September.

Standing overnight repurchase operations run at 4.00 per cent and the overnight reverse repurchase offering rate at 3.75 per cent. The note caps that reverse facility at US$160 billion per counterparty a day.

The Federal Reserve’s own page for the 15 and 16 September meeting lists the statement, the implementation note and the projections. The desk could not open a transcript or a recording of Chairman Warsh’s press conference there.

At the Jackson Hole symposium on 28 August he said the committee must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to its objective, “clearly and at sufficient speed”. He added: “Otherwise, we have work to do.”

In the same speech he said he would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive. He also said the practice of forward guidance “has overstayed its welcome”.

The personal consumption expenditures price index is the gauge the Federal Reserve prefers. It rose 3.7 per cent in the year to July, the Bureau of Economic Analysis reported on 26 August.

The bond market had taken its own view first. The United States Treasury’s daily reading put the ten-year government borrowing rate at 5.00 per cent on 15 September, from 4.97 per cent the day before.

Reuters reported on 16 September that this was a nineteen-year high. TheStreet put the intraday peak at 5.045 per cent and dated the last comparable level to 2007.

American shares ended Tuesday lower, TheStreet reported, with the Standard and Poor’s 500 index at 7,585.73 and down 0.45 per cent. The Dow Jones industrial average closed at 52,093.11 and the Nasdaq composite at 25,981.57.

Ottawa published on the same afternoon as Washington. The Bank of Canada released the summary of its September deliberations on 16 September 2026, covering its decision of 2 September.

That summary says Governing Council decided to leave the policy interest rate unchanged at 2.25 per cent. It says the economy was still in excess supply, with the unemployment rate around 6.5 per cent.

It says consumer price inflation had been hovering around 3 per cent, with the same index excluding gasoline at 2.2 per cent. Core inflation remained around 2 per cent, the summary says.

Members agreed that a spillover from energy prices “could require a monetary policy response to prevent broad-based inflation from setting in”, the summary says. Governing Council decides again on 28 October.

The gap shows up first in the currency. The Bank of Canada’s daily rate put the Canadian dollar at 1.3917 per United States dollar on 15 September, from 1.3909 on 14 September.

Canada’s rate sits 1.50 points below the bottom of the American range. The currency reads that gap before anything else does.

Brussels Offers Ottawa A Word

Ursula von der Leyen gave her State of the European Union address in Strasbourg on Wednesday 16 September. The European Commission’s own page sets it between 9 a.m. and 11.50 a.m. Central European Summer Time.

She told the Parliament she would like to work on “opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU”. BNN Bloomberg and CTV carry that wording, and we could not reach Al Jazeera to check it.

She described a partnership “not against anyone else, but for our common strength”. BNN Bloomberg reported her wish to take the relationship “to the highest level possible”.

Mark Carney sat in the chamber as guest of honour and rose to shake her hand. He addresses the same Parliament himself on Thursday 17 September.

The Prime Minister’s Office published two readouts on 16 September. The first, at 3.37 a.m. New York time, covers his meeting with von der Leyen and Parliament President Roberta Metsola, and names critical minerals, energy, defence, research and development and advanced technologies.

The second, at 10.16 a.m. New York time, covers his bilateral meeting with von der Leyen alone. It says he “welcomed the President’s proposal” to move beyond the existing trade agreement “to a far stronger, more ambitious alliance in the future”.

That second readout lists the ground: critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, artificial intelligence and compute, energy security, space, and financial services and payments. It calls the arrangement “a unique approach that they will define together”.

Canada has not accepted the label. Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador designate to the Union, told reporters “we’re not there” and that the work is about concrete results rather than a name.

He also told reporters that associate membership is “still on the table”, BNN Bloomberg reported. That is a word held open rather than a word refused.

BNN Bloomberg reported that all twenty-seven member states would have to agree, and that no precedent for the status exists. NPR reported that von der Leyen gave no detail on how it would work.

The trade behind it already exists. Von der Leyen told the Parliament in the same address that the existing Canada-Europe agreement has increased trade by 75 per cent in less than a decade.

The reason for the search sits on the southern border. The White House fact sheet of 8 September bans certain Canadian alcoholic beverages and dairy products from the American market on 29 September.

The Council of the European Union sets the next Canada-Europe summit in Montreal on 29 and 30 October 2026. Ottawa has six weeks to decide what it wants the word to mean.

A country accepts a title when it knows what the title obliges it to do.

The War Behind The Fuel Price

The House of Representatives passed a war powers resolution on Tuesday 15 September by 220 votes to 204. Seven Republicans voted for it, the Washington Examiner reported, among them Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania.

The House clerk records the measure as H.Con.Res. 93 and the vote as roll call 307. Its title directs the President to remove American forces from hostilities with Iran.

The measure would still need the Senate. A concurrent resolution is not presented to the President, so it cannot be vetoed, and that is also why it binds nothing.

A chamber can record an objection without ending anything.

The price of the war reaches Americans through a pump. The American Automobile Association put the national diesel average at US$6.3103 a gallon on 16 September, against US$5.9424 a week earlier and US$3.7008 a year earlier.

Regular petrol stood at US$4.3672 a gallon on the same day, against US$3.1862 a year earlier. Those are the association’s own daily averages, not market quotations.

Brent crude settled at US$108.75 a barrel on Tuesday 15 September, with West Texas Intermediate at US$105.83. Those are the exchange settlement series, and Brent closed 2.90 per cent above Monday’s US$105.68.

TheStreet carried intraday prints of US$107.90 and US$104.10 during Tuesday’s session. We carry the settlement rather than an intraday print, because the intraday number moves while the page stands still.

Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said the East-West pipeline came under attack on Thursday 10 September, and shut it as a precaution. The line has stayed shut since. A pipeline is a political object only when it stops.

Washington Refuses Itself

The Senate declined on Tuesday 15 September to advance the Clarity Act, the crypto market bill. Senate roll call vote 234 rejected cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 3633 by 49 to 50, short of the 60 needed.

Four Republicans voted against it on that roll call: Susan Collins, Josh Hawley, Jerry Moran and Thom Tillis. A bill that fails with a majority against it has a longer road back than one that merely runs out of time.

Democrats objected to the bill’s ethics provisions and to the President’s own holdings in the industry, Axios reported. Paul Atkins, chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, said his agency will continue its own rule changes regardless.

The President spent the same Tuesday criticising a court to which he appointed three of the nine justices. Axios reported a Truth Social post of 15 September. We could not open the post at source, so its words are not printed here.

Axios reported that he aimed the criticism at Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett, and praised Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas. The last two had dissented on 14 September.

That order refused to stay the nationwide injunction blocking the Postal Service’s mail-ballot rule. It rested on a finding that the applicant was “unlikely to succeed on the merits”. The case continues, and the midterm elections fall on 3 November.

A government that cannot pass its own bill still finds a bench to blame.

A Network, And An Orbit

The Justice Department announced charges on 15 September against five people it links to Russian intelligence services. The case sits in the Southern District of New York.

Its release names two Russians, Yuri Khrameev, aged 63, and Kirill Khrameev, aged 27. It names two Cubans, Oemis Romagoza Durruthy and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, both aged 35, and Angel Eduardo Castro, aged 22, of Venezuela. All five face a charge of conspiring to finance terrorism.

Three of them also face a charge of conspiring to commit murder for hire. The release says US$40,000 was offered to make a Russian dissident in the United States disappear, and US$25,000 for a target in Lithuania.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said it is the department’s job to stop America’s adversaries from “unleashing violence and terror on American soil”. The department’s own release says: “The defendants remain at large.”

Two days earlier the same government disclosed a capability in public. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink told the Air and Space Forces Association conference on Monday 14 September that the United States has deployed weapons in orbit. Military Times called it the most direct public acknowledgement by an American official so far.

He said it is critically important that the country maintain dominance “not only in the air but in space”, and declined to give numbers or names. Military Times reported that he said disclosing detail would defeat the purpose.

A state announces a weapon when the announcement is the weapon.

The Brake Reaches Brussels

The same Strasbourg address turned to artificial intelligence. Von der Leyen said the chief executives of the most advanced companies are telling governments it is time to slow down on self-recursive models. The Australian Broadcasting Corporation and Euronews both carried that passage.

She proposed that the European Union work with Canada, the United Kingdom and others on evaluating models and on security. It is a government answering a request that the industry made of itself.

Dario Amodei of Anthropic published an essay on Saturday 12 September urging a global slowdown, and Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk agreed on X the same day. Whether von der Leyen had that essay in mind is not something this desk can establish.

Washington has answered differently. Speaker Mike Johnson said on 13 September that developers rather than Congress carry responsibility for safety, and rejected a moratorium.

The proposal also names Canada. Ottawa is being asked to help police a technology it spent this week asking foreign funds to build on its territory.

A government reaches for a brake most readily when the driver has asked for one.

The Questions Left Open

The Federal Reserve’s own page for the 15 and 16 September meeting lists the statement, the implementation note and the projections. The desk could not open a transcript or a recording of Chairman Warsh’s press conference there.

The statement records a 12 to 0 vote, and the desk found no named voting list on it. Why the committee published a tally without names is not something this desk can establish.

The legal status of a European associate membership is still undefined, though its content is not. The second readout names the fields it would cover. NPR reported that von der Leyen gave no detail on how the status itself would work. We found no member state saying publicly whether it would agree.

We could not establish whether von der Leyen’s remarks on slowing artificial intelligence referred to any particular executive. She named no company, in the accounts we read.

A committee that raises into an oil shock is defending its own word.

What This Means From Latin America

The range set at 2 p.m. New York time sets the price of dollar borrowing for every government and company in this hemisphere. Nobody in Brasília, Bogotá or Lima had a vote in that room.

Diesel at US$6.3103 a gallon on 16 September is the freight cost that carries Brazilian soy and Chilean fruit northward. Food prices in this region follow that number after a delay of weeks.

Canada spent today being offered a second market, two weeks before American import bans on its alcohol and dairy take effect. Several countries in this region have made the same calculation with less ceremony.

The Justice Department’s indictment of 15 September names two Cuban nationals and one Venezuelan among five defendants. Latin American passports are becoming useful to services that are not Latin American.

What We Are Watching

Chairman Warsh at the microphone — the Federal Reserve’s own page for the 15 and 16 September meeting lists the statement, the implementation note and the projections. The desk could not open a transcript or a recording of the press conference there.

Go Deeper. The web dossier carries the full deep dive on the Federal Reserve’s decision and three ways the next six months can run. It also carries a health check of the continent, the North American calendar and today’s verification notes.

More from the Rio Times Intelligence Desk on 16 September 2026: Africa · Asia · Europe. For how these stories developed, see the USA & Canada Intelligence Brief for 15 September and 14 September.

North American politics and trade policy and their bearing on this hemisphere run through our pillar coverage of The United States & Canada.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Federal Reserve decide, and what does it change?

The Federal Open Market Committee raised the target range for the federal funds rate by a quarter point, to 3.75 to 4.00 per cent. Its statement of 16 September 2026 was released at 2 p.m. New York time and says the move comes “in support of the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate”. The same statement says the committee “approved the following statement for release by a 12 – 0 vote”. The desk read that release and found no named voting list on it, so no individual voter is named here. The range had stood at 3.50 to 3.75 per cent since the statement of 10 December 2025. The five committee statements of 2026 before today each said maintain. The stated reason is one sentence: “Inflation remains elevated.” The statement adds that “Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal”. The Summary of Economic Projections, released at the same hour, puts the median federal funds rate at 4.1 per cent for the end of 2026. It puts 3.9 per cent for the end of 2028, against 3.8 and 3.4 per cent in June. The implementation note sets interest on reserve balances at 3.90 per cent and the primary credit rate at 4.00 per cent, both effective 17 September. Before the decision Reuters reported on 16 September that pricing stood above 90 per cent. Kiplinger reported the CME FedWatch measure at 92.7 per cent, read on 15 September. A higher American rate raises the cost of dollar borrowing across Latin America, and it raises the return on holding dollars rather than local currency.

What would associate membership of the European Union mean for Canada?

Its content is sketched; its legal form is not. Ursula von der Leyen spoke to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on 16 September 2026. She said she would like to work on “opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU”. She described a partnership “not against anyone else, but for our common strength”. BNN Bloomberg and CTV carry that wording; we could not reach Al Jazeera to check it. BNN Bloomberg reported that no precedent for the status exists and that all twenty-seven member states would have to agree, and NPR reported that she gave no detail on how it would work. The Prime Minister’s Office published two readouts on 16 September. The bilateral one, at 10.16 a.m. New York time, says Mark Carney “welcomed the President’s proposal” to move beyond the existing trade agreement. It names critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, artificial intelligence and compute, energy security, space, and financial services and payments. It calls it “a unique approach that they will define together”. Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador designate to the Union, told reporters the same day that Canada is “not there” but that the label is “still on the table”. Von der Leyen said the existing agreement has increased trade by 75 per cent in less than a decade. The two sides meet in Montreal on 29 and 30 October 2026.

Why are American fuel prices still rising?

Supply, not demand, is doing the work. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said the East-West pipeline, the line that carries crude away from the Strait of Hormuz, came under attack on Thursday 10 September, and shut it as a precaution. The line has stayed shut since. Brent crude settled at US$108.75 a barrel on Tuesday 15 September, with West Texas Intermediate at US$105.83. Those are the exchange settlement series, and Brent closed 2.90 per cent above Monday’s US$105.68. TheStreet carried intraday prints of US$107.90 and US$104.10 during Tuesday’s session; we carry settlements rather than intraday prints, because the intraday figure changes inside the same page. The American Automobile Association put the national diesel average at US$6.3103 a gallon on 16 September. That is against US$5.9424 a week earlier and US$3.7008 a year earlier, with regular petrol at US$4.3672. Diesel is the number that reaches a Latin American shopper, because it sets the cost of moving food.

What did the desk fail to establish today?

Four things. The Federal Reserve’s own page for the 15 and 16 September meeting lists the statement, the implementation note and the projections. The desk could not open a transcript or a recording of Chairman Kevin Warsh’s press conference there. Nothing from that press conference appears in this edition. The statement records a 12 to 0 vote, and the desk found no named voting list on it. No individual voter is named here, and no dissent is reported. The legal status of a European associate membership is undefined, though the bilateral readout names the fields it would cover. NPR reported that Ursula von der Leyen gave no detail on how the status itself would work. Neither readout announced a treaty text. We found no member state saying publicly whether it would agree. And we could not establish whether von der Leyen’s remarks on slowing work at the artificial intelligence frontier referred to any particular executive, because she named no company in the accounts we read. Where we do not know, we say so, and we correct in the open when we are wrong.

The full Africa Intelligence Dossier — the editor’s leader, the deep dive, the country health check and the people who matter — is updated daily by the Rio Times Intelligence Desk. Open the dossier · The dossier archive

Washington announced a visa restriction policy aimed at South Africans on Tuesday, 15 September, over laws the South African parliament passed. Pretoria answered in writing, through a spokesman, and the two documents passed each other.

Four of the day’s decisions about Africa were taken in Washington, Geneva, Budapest and Cairo. What the continent settled for itself was smaller, and carried prices.

Read in English, French, Arabic, Portuguese and Swahili, across the continent’s largest outlets and our own Africa desk.

South Africa: Washington Puts A Policy On A List

The United States Department of State announced a new visa restriction policy on Tuesday, 15 September. Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued the statement, and it names South Africa.

It covers people responsible for, or complicit in, laws that enable uncompensated land seizures or race-based discrimination. The incitement of imminent violence is also named, and certain family members may be restricted.

The statement said: “The United States will not allow such behavior to go unchecked.” Rubio wrote separately on X that those responsible for these injustices “have no place in the United States”.

Politicsweb, carrying the statement on 16 September, gives the instrument as section 212(a)(3)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. That clause lets the Secretary of State bar a foreign national on foreign policy grounds.

Independent Online reported on 16 September that the announcement named no individuals, and the Daily Maverick that its sources expect no public list. Leo Brent Bozell III, the United States ambassador, called the policy “only the first step in a series of escalatory measures” in the same Daily Maverick report.

Ronald Lamola, the Minister of International Relations and Cooperation, raised concern at the unilateral character of the measure. Eyewitness News reported his department’s reply on 16 September, given through its spokesman Chrispin Phiri.

BusinessTech reported on 11 September that Washington has put five demands to Pretoria, first in June 2025 and again in March 2026. They cover farm violence, hate speech, compensation for expropriation, black economic empowerment and alignment with Iran.

Thuli Madonsela, a former Public Protector, said on X that the American account is inaccurate, in remarks Cape Town Etc carried on 16 September. She said: “Black deprivation is not an accident of history or misfortune.”

President Cyril Ramaphosa assented to the Expropriation Act on 23 January 2025. A sovereign law now carries a foreign penalty attached to a passport.

South Africa: Two Files That Stay At Home

Police found an eighth woman’s body in Ekurhuleni on Tuesday, 15 September, behind Club 69 in KwaThema, Springs. The Daily Maverick set out the sequence on 16 September.

The first was found near the R21 road at Kempton Park on 15 July, the second there on 24 August, then two on 7 September. Three more followed on 10, 12 and 14 September, one of them Elizabeth Moselakgomo, who was 38.

Firoz Cachalia, the acting Minister of Police, announced a high-level team on 15 September, with Gauteng premier Panyaza Lesufi and the acting national commissioner, Lieutenant General Puleng Dimpane. He said the team is in place and has the expertise for such cases.

The reward stands at 400,000 rand, about US$24,500 at the rate CNBC Africa reported for 15 September. One suspect has been in custody since 17 July over the first death, reportedly her partner.

TimesLIVE reported on 16 September that police call similarities between some cases concerning, while cautioning that it is too early to conclude one person killed the women. Only two of the eight have been publicly named.

TimesLIVE’s list of the same day includes Itumeleng Kekana, found at Pomona on 3 August, and records one discovery on 7 September where the Daily Maverick records two. Both outlets count eight.

Ramaphosa said on 15 September that he had directed the cases be prioritised. He asked that “no stone be left unturned in bringing those responsible to justice”.

The Madlanga Commission resumed on Tuesday, 15 September, its 173rd day, after a recess begun on 3 September. Its subject that morning was the infiltration of the Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department by criminal networks.

The commission examines criminality, political interference and corruption in the criminal justice system, and reports to Ramaphosa by 16 November 2026. A state is read abroad through its statutes and at home through its case files.

Nigeria: The Truce In The Video, The Price In The Table

The New Humanitarian reported on 7 September that the government and a Boko Haram faction had agreed a secret ceasefire. Al Jazeera carried the account on 9 September.

The reported terms were three months from June, with a possible forty-day extension. Some 360 villagers taken from Ngoshe in March were released, and five billion naira was said to have been paid.

Al Jazeera glossed that sum at US$3.7 million and said it could not verify the ceasefire or the payment. The account rested on three unnamed people with contacts among Boko Haram members, and the government denies paying a ransom.

A seven-minute video released on Sunday, 13 September, answered it. In it Mallam Abdulrahman, described as the group’s Sharia judge, called the reported reconciliation “a lie”.

HumAngle reported the video on 14 September, and Premium Times carried it on 15 September. The Star of Nigeria, reporting the same day, gave the release date.

Bayo Onanuga, the presidential spokesman, said only the National Security Adviser’s office or the Defence Ministry could address the matter. Premium Times said the adviser’s spokesman did not respond to its requests for comment.

The Guardian reported on 8 September that Major General Mike Onoja, director of defence media operations, declined to comment on the report. The question has now been passed between three offices.

Malik Samuel, a researcher quoted by Al Jazeera, said any such arrangement could be tactical and temporary. President Bola Tinubu has refused negotiation in public and announced 30,000 further military recruits.

The National Bureau of Statistics put headline inflation at 15.39 per cent in August, from 15.43 per cent in July. It published on Tuesday, 15 September, and the rate a year earlier was 23.14 per cent.

Food inflation was 19.57 per cent over the year, from 20.31 per cent, and core inflation 13.29 per cent, from 14.97 per cent. Prices rose 0.71 per cent over the month, against 1.57 per cent in July.

Abuja can show a slowing price index and an unsettled account of its own war. Only one of the two has a published method.

The Red Sea: A Pipeline, A Price And The Boats To Obock

Houthi forces took the port of Mocha on 10 September and Yemen’s Red Sea coast the next day, Al Jazeera reported. That places Bab al-Mandeb, the strait at the southern mouth of the Red Sea, under their control.

Drones launched from Iraq’s Maysan province struck Saudi Arabia’s East–West crude pipeline on Thursday, 10 September. Saudi Arabia announced the closure on Friday, 11 September, and later suspended loadings at Yanbu.

Al Jazeera reported on 12 September that no group had claimed the attack, and put the line at four to five million barrels a day. The 1,200-kilometre line was built to move crude to the Red Sea without passing the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude for November settled at US$108.75 a barrel on Tuesday, 15 September, against US$105.68 on Monday. That is a rise of 2.9 per cent, and The Rio Times called it the highest close in nearly four months.

Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince, went to Cairo on 15 September and met President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. The Egyptian presidency said Gulf security is an integral part of Egypt’s national security.

Ossama Rabie, chairman of the Suez Canal Authority, put revenue for the 2025/2026 financial year at US$4.67 billion, 23 per cent above the year before. Egyptian Streets reported his television interview on 30 June, against a 2023 figure of US$9.4 billion.

Al Jazeera reported on 13 September that Red Sea traffic volume and tonnage fell between 50 and 55 per cent from 2023 to 2025. It cited International Monetary Fund port data, and the route round the Cape of Good Hope adds more than twenty days.

The United Nations refugee agency said on 15 September that more than 2,400 people had crossed to Djibouti in four days. They landed at Obock, Khor Angar, Moulhoule and Godoria, and most were women, children and older people.

Djibouti’s government put arrivals above 3,400 in 48 hours, through its state news agency on Sunday, 13 September. Al Jazeera carried that figure on 15 September.

The International Organization for Migration gave more than 85,000 displaced inside Yemen, also on 13 September. The refugee agency’s own figure, in its statement of 15 September, was more than 100,000.

Alexandre Coissac of the International Organization for Migration said that if arrivals continue at this rate “we’ll not be able to manage”. The strait charges twice, once at the pump and once at the shore.

DR Congo And Rwanda: Two Delegations In Geneva

The seventh meeting of the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism opens in Geneva on Wednesday, 16 September, and runs to 17 September. The sixth meeting, held on 12 and 13 August, fixed the date.

Delegations from DR Congo and Rwanda attend, with the United States, Qatar, Togo for the African Union and the African Union Commission. The mechanism monitors the Washington Accords.

Those accords were signed on 4 December 2025 and reaffirmed a peace agreement of 27 June 2025. Kinshasa undertook to neutralise the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda, a Rwandan Hutu armed group in eastern Congo.

Kigali undertook to disengage its forces, and the August meeting agreed two monitoring initiatives and a planning conference in October. Al Jazeera reported on 15 September that the security commitments remain unfulfilled and fighting continues.

M23 took Goma and Bukavu in 2025, Al Jazeera reported on 15 September. Whatever Geneva agrees will be published after this edition closes.

Kenya: A Price Held, A Championship Won

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority left maximum pump prices unchanged for 15 September to 14 October. Super petrol stays at 214.03 shillings a litre and diesel at 217.86.

At the 129.47 shillings to the dollar The Rio Times reported on 4 September, that is about US$1.65 and US$1.68 a litre. The landed cost of petrol fell 7.87 per cent while diesel rose 11.86 per cent.

The authority called the movements divergent and pointed to transport costs, margins, taxes and levies in its formula. Joseph Oketch, its acting director general, signed the notice on 14 September.

World Athletics gave Nairobi the 2029 World Athletics Championships on Tuesday, 15 September, at a council meeting in Budapest. It is the first time the championships go to Africa.

Nairobi beat London for 2029, and the venue is the Moi International Sports Centre at Kasarani. Sebastian Coe, the World Athletics president, said: “Nairobi presented a compelling and emotional bid.”

Munich takes 2031 and Beijing hosts 2027. One Kenyan decision holds for a month, the other for three years.

Senegal And The Continent: Two Counts Of Disease

Senegal’s Ministry of Health and Public Hygiene said on 14 September that the country had 76 confirmed diphtheria cases and nine deaths. The count ran to 13 September, across 24 health districts in 11 regions.

Diphtheria is a bacterial infection of the throat, preventable by vaccination, and Kédougou carries 28 of the cases. The count stood at 57 cases and eight deaths five days earlier, on 8 September.

The World Health Organization recorded 1,153 confirmed mpox cases and seven deaths in 11 African countries between 6 July and 16 August. Premium Times summarised the report on 15 September, and Madagascar accounted for 785 of the cases.

Angola recorded 184 and Kenya 94. Since 1 January 2025, 35 African countries have reported 52,424 confirmed cases and 238 deaths.

The organisation said weekly confirmed cases have held near 200, and that the figures could be underestimated because of reporting delays. A steady count may describe a tired counter rather than a steady disease.

What This Means From Latin America

The Department of State restricted visas for Brazilian judicial officials and their immediate family members in July 2025. The subject then was a country’s courts, and the subject now is a country’s land law.

The International Fund for Agricultural Development reported on 14 September that migrants sent US$728.6 billion to low and middle-income countries in 2025. Latin America and the Caribbean received US$168.6 billion of it and Africa US$124.2 billion.

Brent at US$108.75 is revenue for Brazilian and Colombian producers and a bill for importers in Nairobi and Antananarivo. The same barrel reads as income on one coast of the Atlantic and as a subsidy question on the other.

What We Are Watching

Geneva’s seventh meeting — whether the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism publishes a joint statement when it closes on 17 September, as the sixth did in August.

— whether the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism publishes a joint statement when it closes on 17 September, as the sixth did in August. The visa list — whether any South African is refused entry, after the Daily Maverick reported that its sources expect no published names.

— whether any South African is refused entry, after the Daily Maverick reported that its sources expect no published names. The Ekurhuleni investigation — whether police connect the eight deaths found since 15 July, after calling the similarities between some of them concerning.

— whether police connect the eight deaths found since 15 July, after calling the similarities between some of them concerning. Abuja’s security adviser — whether his office addresses the reported ceasefire that the presidential spokesman referred to it on 15 September.

— whether his office addresses the reported ceasefire that the presidential spokesman referred to it on 15 September. Yanbu and the East–West line — how long Saudi Arabia keeps the pipeline and the loadings shut, which is what the Brent settlement is pricing.

— how long Saudi Arabia keeps the pipeline and the loadings shut, which is what the Brent settlement is pricing. Kenya’s next fuel review — the notice due on 14 October, the first to carry September’s crude into Kenyan pump prices.

— the notice due on 14 October, the first to carry September’s crude into Kenyan pump prices. Senegal’s diphtheria count — which rose from 57 cases on 8 September to 76 on 13 September, in the ministry’s own figures.

The Bigger Picture Four rooms outside Africa decided African questions this week. A visa policy in Washington, a security mechanism in Geneva, a host city in Budapest, a sea lane in Cairo. What the continent settled for itself was a pump price, a price index and two disease counts. The canal earned US$4.67 billion in 2025/2026 against US$9.4 billion in 2023. What the desk could not establish is large. We do not know who is on the American list, whether the eight Ekurhuleni deaths are one case, or what terms bind Nigeria and the faction in the video. Three bodies counted the Djibouti crossing over different windows, and each count is carried above with its date. For a reader with money or family in these places, fuel, visas and vaccination records all moved this week.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly did the United States announce about South Africa, and whom does it affect?

The Department of State announced a new visa restriction policy on Tuesday, 15 September, in a statement by Secretary of State Marco Rubio. It applies to foreign nationals responsible for, or complicit in, laws or policies that enable uncompensated land seizures, race-based discrimination, or the incitement of imminent violence, and certain family members may also be restricted. Politicsweb, carrying the statement on 16 September, gives the instrument as section 212(a)(3)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. Independent Online reported that no individuals were named, and the Daily Maverick that its sources expect no public list.

Is there a ceasefire between Nigeria and Boko Haram?

That is unresolved. The New Humanitarian reported on 7 September that the government and a faction had agreed a secret ceasefire. The reported terms ran three months from June, with a possible forty-day extension, and 360 villagers taken from Ngoshe in March were released. Its account rested on three unnamed people with contacts among Boko Haram members. Al Jazeera carried the report on 9 September and said it could not verify the ceasefire or the payment of five billion naira, glossed at US$3.7 million. The government denies paying a ransom. On 15 September Premium Times reported a video in which Mallam Abdulrahman, described as the group’s Sharia judge, called the reported reconciliation “a lie”.

Why did Brent crude rise, and what does it do to African fuel bills?

Drones launched from Iraq’s Maysan province struck Saudi Arabia’s East–West crude pipeline on Thursday, 10 September. Saudi Arabia announced the closure on Friday, 11 September, and later suspended loadings at Yanbu. Al Jazeera reported on 12 September that the pipeline carries four to five million barrels a day. Brent crude for November settled at US$108.75 a barrel on Tuesday, 15 September, against US$105.68 on Monday, a rise of 2.9 per cent. Oil exporters such as Nigeria and Angola receive more for each barrel, while importers pay more for refined fuel. Kenya’s Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority held its pump prices to 14 October, so September’s crude reaches Kenyan pumps in the next notice.

How many people have crossed from Yemen to Djibouti, and why do the numbers differ?

Three bodies counted different windows, and this brief carries each with its source and date. The United Nations refugee agency said on 15 September that more than 2,400 people had crossed in four days. More than 60 per cent were women, children and older people. Djibouti’s government put arrivals above 3,400 within 48 hours, through its state news agency on Sunday, 13 September. Al Jazeera carried that figure on 15 September. On displacement inside Yemen the refugee agency gives more than 100,000, and the International Organization for Migration more than 85,000 on 13 September.
