Asia spent Wednesday handing its arguments to judges. Four capitals moved a decision they could not take themselves into a courtroom.

Seoul settled a bus dispute by postponing the number at its centre, and Manila took a former Speaker’s plunder plea. Bangkok had sent 77 people to its Supreme Court on Monday 14 September. A referral buys time, and time is what each of these cities wanted.

Read in English and Korean, across the region’s largest outlets, each capital’s own press and our own Asia desk.

South Korea: A Settlement At Ten To Two

Seoul’s bus union and its operators reached a wage deal at 1:50 a.m. Seoul time on Wednesday, about two hours before a full strike was due. Talks had run for roughly twelve hours.

Pay rises 3.2 per cent for 2026, against 2.9 per cent in 2025, the Korea Herald reported on 16 September. The city government puts the cost of each percentage point at about 14 billion won (about US$10.3 million) a year.

The argument underneath the money was never settled. The union wanted ordinary hourly pay calculated on 176 hours a month, with a 7.85 per cent rise, which the operators and the city said would lift pay by about 16 per cent.

Both sides agreed instead to wait for the Supreme Court, which they expect to rule on ordinary wages by the end of the year. The desk could not find a published hearing date.

Park Jeom-gon, who leads the drivers’ union, told the Korea JoongAng Daily the deal “isn’t entirely satisfying, but we tried not to go on strike for the sake of citizens”. The operators’ association head, Kim Jeong-hwan, called it “a big burden for both labor and management”.

About 7,400 buses run by 64 companies carry some 3.8 million passengers a day, and 1,500 free shuttle buses were stood down before dawn. Wednesday would have been the capital’s second citywide walkout in eight months, after a 44-hour strike in January ended without agreement on the calculation method. A city that cannot agree on a divisor can still agree on a date.

Seoul: Five Presidents And An Open Currency

The same city hosted the first Korea-Central Asia summit at the level of leaders on Wednesday. Presidents Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Sadyr Japarov, Emomali Rahmon, Serdar Berdimuhamedov and Shavkat Mirziyoyev met President Lee Jae-myung and adopted a Seoul Declaration.

Lee told the meeting that the “Silk Road spirit” of Central Asia “is more necessary than ever”, the Korea Times reported. The stated aim is to join the region’s minerals to Korean exploration and processing.

Korea also opened its currency a little further. From 16 September the finance ministry lets registered foreign institutions settle won abroad. The reporting threshold for won borrowing rises from 30 billion won to 100 billion won, the Seoul Economic Daily reported on 16 September. That is about US$22 million to US$73 million on the desk’s conversion.

The Seoul Central District Court then ordered North Korea to pay 44.6 billion won (about US$32.5 million). The sum covers the demolition of the joint liaison office at Kaesong on 16 June 2020, in a case the unification ministry brought in 2023.

One capital spent a single day settling a strike, signing a declaration and opening a currency. Ambition and unease often keep the same office hours.

China: More Made, Less Bought

The National Bureau of Statistics of China published August activity on 15 September. Industrial output rose 5.2 per cent on a year earlier, after 4.5 per cent in July.

Retail sales rose 0.4 per cent, against 0.6 per cent in July and 1.0 per cent in June. Fixed-asset investment fell 7.2 per cent in the first eight months, after 6.7 per cent through July.

A Reuters poll of 42 analysts had looked for output at 4.8 per cent and sales at 0.8 per cent. The factories beat that forecast and the shops missed it.

The bureau said the economy “was generally stable” in August, while “the domestic imbalance between strong supply and weak demand is still acute”. That is an unusually plain sentence from a statistical office.

Jiang Bin of China’s Ministry of National Defense objected to Orient Shield 26, a Japanese, American and Australian exercise running from 8 to 24 September. He said it advances “the deployment of long-range offensive weapons under the guise of a ‘shield'”, in remarks China Daily carried on 15 September.

At the foreign ministry’s briefing that day, spokesperson Guo Jiakun traced the trouble with Tokyo to Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s “erroneous words and deeds on Taiwan”. A country that makes more and buys less exports its own caution.

Japan: A Defence Figure Still Under Discussion

Japan is weighing a defence budget worth 3.5 per cent of national output, Bloomberg reported, with 3 per cent as a lower option. The report rests on people familiar with the matter who asked not to be named.

Defence spending this fiscal year is 10.6 trillion yen (about US$68 billion). Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said in April that this was 1.9 per cent of nominal output in 2022. Against the Cabinet Office’s forecast for this fiscal year it is 1.5 per cent. A 3.5 per cent budget on that forecast would be near 24 trillion yen (about US$155 billion).

Elbridge Colby, the American under secretary of defense for policy, said in August that Washington is “anxiously looking for Japan to step up”. Bloomberg describes 3.5 per cent as a figure under consideration in Sanae Takaichi’s government, not one it has announced.

The Bank of Japan meets on 17 and 18 September, on its own published schedule. It set the overnight call rate at around 1.0 per cent on 16 June, and held there on 31 July by eight votes to one.

Takata Hajime was the single dissenter in July, proposing around 1.25 per cent. A Reuters poll reported on 9 September found economists expect a rise to around 1.25 per cent this month. That is a forecast rather than a decision.

The health ministry counted 107,677 people aged 100 or over on 1 September, the first time above 100,000 since records began in 1963. About nine in ten are women, and a state buying missiles is also counting centenarians.

Thailand: The Vote Inside The Vote

Thailand’s Election Commission referred 77 people to the Supreme Court’s Election Cases Division on 14 September, over the Senate selection of June 2024. Twenty-six are sitting senators, 36 were eligible to vote in the selection, and 15 are others.

They were drawn from 427 people originally accused, on Nation Thailand’s reporting of 14 and 15 September. The chairman, Narong Klunwarin, said the referral does not establish guilt.

The Election Commission Office also disclosed, on 15 September, its individual votes on 21 Bhumjaithai figures it declined to prosecute. It cleared twelve of them by five votes to two, two by six to one and seven unanimously.

Nation Thailand published the commission’s voting table on 16 September. It records Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and Newin Chidchob at five to two, and the party secretary-general Chaichanok Chidchob unanimously. Commissioner Sitthichot Intrawises has given the reasoning of the minority, which rests on the Thai Examiner alone.

In Singapore on 15 September, Thailand and Cambodia opened a compulsory conciliation over about 26,000 square kilometres of seabed. The panel sits at the Permanent Court of Arbitration, may take a year, and cannot bind either government.

A chamber accused of choosing itself has asked judges to decide who chose it. Institutions under suspicion rarely pick their own witnesses.

The Philippines: A Former Speaker Pleads By Video

Martin Romualdez, until recently Speaker of the House of Representatives, pleaded not guilty to plunder before the Sandiganbayan on Wednesday. He appeared by videoconference from the New Quezon City Jail at Payatas, in a wheelchair, the court’s Third Division having granted his motion. His lawyer, Ade Fajardo, said Romualdez “is maintaining his innocence”.

The charge covers 7.44 billion pesos in alleged kickbacks on projects funded between 2022 and 2025, the Philippine Daily Inquirer reported on 14 September. The Associated Press gave the sum on 16 September as 7.4 billion pesos, about US$118 million.

He was moved to the New Quezon City Jail at Payatas at 10:49 p.m. Manila time on 14 September. Three others are charged with him, and the former representative Zaldy Co is a fugitive in Europe.

Nearly 10,000 flood-control projects worth more than US$9 billion have been let since President Ferdinand Marcos Jr took office in mid-2022, the Associated Press reported. Many were found substandard, overpriced or never built.

The Senate impeachment court spent Monday and Tuesday on the charge of unexplained wealth against Vice-President Sara Duterte. Senator Francis Escudero, presiding on Tuesday, allowed her asset declarations from 2007 to be shown to establish a baseline.

The Anti-Money Laundering Council reported transactions involving her and her husband totalling 6.77 billion pesos between 2006 and 2025. The Philippine Star stressed that this is an aggregate over two decades, not a sum held at any one moment.

The Quiet Files: Jakarta, Kuala Lumpur, New Delhi

Indonesia’s currency has weakened for four sessions running. The rupiah stood at 17,677.90 per US dollar on 15 September, against a previous close of 17,654.00, on Trading Economics data read on 16 September.

Suahasil Nazara, finance minister since 14 September, has promised a budget deficit below 3 per cent. Bank Indonesia takes its next rate decision on 23 September, with its policy rate at 5.75 per cent.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim wrote on 15 September that Malaysia “will not allow our country to be used as a conduit” for shipments supporting Israel’s military capabilities. Suspicious cargo will be inspected under Malaysian law, he wrote.

Malaysia’s foreign ministry said on 14 September that 55 Malaysians remain uncontactable after floods and landslides in Nepal and China. The count stood at 91 at the end of August, 55 in Nepal and 36 in China, and fell as people were traced. Its rescue team left nine drones with Nepal’s disaster authority.

In New Delhi, the external affairs ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal spoke on 15 September about Narendra Modi’s meeting with Xi Jinping. Modi urged China to be guided by the “three mutuals”: mutual respect, mutual interest and mutual sensitivity.

Bangladesh sold US$806.46 million of ready-made garments to the United States in August, 25.65 per cent more than in July, on Export Promotion Bureau figures. Brent‘s previous close was US$108.75 a barrel on Trading Economics data read on 16 September.

What We Could Not Establish

Four questions in this edition remain open, and we would rather say so. We do not yet know what the Bank of Japan will decide on Friday, and the Reuters poll is a forecast.

The reported Chinese warning over Xi Jinping’s Washington visit still rests on a single Kyodo News report carried by the Taipei Times on 13 September. The foreign ministry transcript of 15 September records no question on it, which is not a denial.

Commissioner Sitthichot Intrawises’s account of why two commissioners dissented in Thailand rests on the Thai Examiner of 16 September. The vote counts themselves are an official disclosure.

The desk could not find a published hearing date for Korea’s Supreme Court ruling on ordinary wages. Both sides of the bus dispute expect it by the end of the year.

What This Means From Latin America

Korea’s summit with five Central Asian presidents is a minerals conversation before it is a diplomatic one. Chile, Peru and Argentina sell into the same buyers, and a second supply route changes the price of the first.

China made more in August and sold less at home, which points surplus output outwards. Brazilian and Mexican manufacturers have met that pattern before, and it arrives as cheaper imports rather than as news.

If the Bank of Japan makes borrowing dearer on Friday, money borrowed cheaply in yen becomes costlier to hold elsewhere. Unwinding those positions has moved the Brazilian real and the Mexican peso in past cycles.

The deepest parallel is the courtroom. Latin America has spent a decade watching corruption cases test whether institutions can try the people who built them.

What We Are Watching

The Bank of Japan on Friday — whether it moves from around 1.0 per cent, set on 16 June, to around 1.25 per cent. A Reuters poll reported on 9 September found economists expect that, and what the bank says about 29 and 30 October matters more.

A Reuters poll reported on 9 September found economists expect that, and what the bank says about 29 and 30 October matters more. The Federal Reserve — its decision was due at 2 p.m. New York time on Wednesday, after this brief closed. Asian currencies traded all day against an outcome nobody yet had.

— its decision was due at 2 p.m. New York time on Wednesday, after this brief closed. Asian currencies traded all day against an outcome nobody yet had. President Lee’s news conference — 90 minutes at 10 a.m. Seoul time on Friday 18 September at Yeongbingwan, his seventh. Realmeter put his approval at 33.8 per cent on 14 September, and Gallup Korea’s reading published on 11 September was 38 per cent.

— 90 minutes at 10 a.m. Seoul time on Friday 18 September at Yeongbingwan, his seventh. Realmeter put his approval at 33.8 per cent on 14 September, and Gallup Korea’s reading published on 11 September was 38 per cent. Korea’s Supreme Court on ordinary wages — the ruling both sides of the bus dispute agreed to wait for, expected by the end of the year. It decides whether 176 hours or 209 governs a large part of Korean overtime pay.

— the ruling both sides of the bus dispute agreed to wait for, expected by the end of the year. It decides whether 176 hours or 209 governs a large part of Korean overtime pay. Thailand’s Election Cases Division — whether it accepts the 77 referrals, and whether the names become public. The Election Commission Office published its individual votes on 15 September, with twelve of 21 respondents cleared five to two.

— whether it accepts the 77 referrals, and whether the names become public. The Election Commission Office published its individual votes on 15 September, with twelve of 21 respondents cleared five to two. Bank Indonesia on 23 September — whether a policy rate of 5.75 per cent holds while the rupiah sits near 17,678 per US dollar. It is the new finance minister’s first test from the outside.

— whether a policy rate of 5.75 per cent holds while the rupiah sits near 17,678 per US dollar. It is the new finance minister’s first test from the outside. Xi Jinping’s Washington visit on 24 September — whether it happens, and whether Washington first approves a US$14 billion package of missiles and interceptors. Focus Taiwan reported on 4 August that Representative Michael McCaul expected the package to go to Congress soon. The foreign ministry’s briefings of 15 September raised no question on the visit.

— whether it happens, and whether Washington first approves a US$14 billion package of missiles and interceptors. Focus Taiwan reported on 4 August that Representative Michael McCaul expected the package to go to Congress soon. The foreign ministry’s briefings of 15 September raised no question on the visit. The Philippine Ombudsman — Jesus Crispin Remulla has said more flood-control cases are coming. Nearly 10,000 such projects worth more than US$9 billion have been let since mid-2022.

The Bigger Picture Asia built its reputation on being able to decide quickly. Wednesday showed a region that has learned to decide slowly and in public instead. A wage formula went to a supreme court, a senate went to a supreme court, and a former speaker went to an anti-graft bench. Each transfer costs time and buys a legitimacy that speed cannot. This is the late part of a long cycle rather than the start of a crisis. Korea, Thailand and the Philippines all industrialised under governments that decided first and explained afterwards. What follows such phases is usually duller than either the alarm or the boom implied. Readers who hold that in mind can watch a week like this one without moving.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Seoul’s bus strike actually happen?

No. The union and the operators reached a wage deal at 1:50 a.m. Seoul time on Wednesday 16 September, about two hours before the strike was due to begin with the first departures at 4 a.m. Seoul time. Buses ran on their ordinary timetable, and the 1,500 free shuttle buses the city had prepared were stood down. Pay rises 3.2 per cent for 2026, against 2.9 per cent in 2025. The dispute that caused the standoff, whether monthly ordinary pay is calculated on 176 hours or 209, was not resolved. Both sides agreed to wait for a Supreme Court ruling on ordinary wages, which the Korea Herald reported on 16 September they expect by the end of the year.

Why does one number in a wage formula matter so much?

Because the divisor sets the price of every extra hour. Monthly pay divided by 176 hours produces a higher hourly rate than the same pay divided by 209. Overtime, night work and holiday work are all multiples of that hourly rate. The union sought 176 hours together with a 7.85 per cent rise, and the operators and the city said that would raise pay by about 16 per cent in practice. The city government puts the cost of a single percentage point of bus pay at about 14 billion won, roughly US$10.3 million, a year. The same question sits under wage bargaining across Korean industry, which is why both sides preferred a court.

What did China’s August figures actually show?

A widening gap between what China produces and what it consumes. The National Bureau of Statistics of China reported on 15 September that industrial output in August rose 5.2 per cent on a year earlier, up from 4.5 per cent in July. Retail sales rose 0.4 per cent, down from 0.6 per cent in July and 1.0 per cent in June. Fixed-asset investment fell 7.2 per cent in the first eight months, against a 6.7 per cent fall through July. A Reuters poll of 42 analysts had expected output at 4.8 per cent and retail sales at 0.8 per cent. The factories beat that forecast and the shops missed it, and the bureau’s own release said the imbalance between strong supply and weak demand remains pronounced.

What does any of this change for someone living in Latin America?

Three things, in plain terms. First, Chinese factories running ahead of Chinese shoppers push surplus goods outwards, and Brazilian and Mexican manufacturers usually feel that as cheaper competing imports within a few months. Second, a Reuters poll reported on 9 September found economists expect the Bank of Japan to raise its policy rate on 18 September. If it does, money borrowed cheaply in yen and invested elsewhere becomes more expensive to hold, and unwinding those positions has moved the Brazilian real and the Mexican peso in past cycles. Third, Korea’s new minerals conversation with five Central Asian states adds a competing supply route for materials that Chile, Peru and Argentina sell. None of these is a reason to act today, and all three are reasons to read the next quarter closely.

Sources: The Korea Herald, Korea JoongAng Daily, Seoul Economic Daily, SBS News and The Korea Times. Also The Elec, UPI, Taipei Times and The Jakarta Post. And China Daily, Business Recorder, Euronews, Nation Thailand and Thai Examiner. Also Asia News Network carrying The Straits Times, Philippine Star and Philippine Daily Inquirer. And Manila Bulletin, Malay Mail, The Daily Star and Focus Taiwan. Those outlets carried reports from Bloomberg, Reuters, Kyodo News, Agence France-Presse, Asian News International and the Associated Press. Primary documents: the Bank of Japan’s statements on monetary policy of 16 June and 31 July 2026 and its published meeting schedule. Also the National Bureau of Statistics of China’s English release of 15 September 2026. And the Chinese foreign ministry’s press conference transcript of the same date. Reporting from 11 to 16 September 2026. Currency conversions are desk calculations against rates checked on 16 September 2026 and are approximate.

The full Europe Intelligence Dossier is updated daily by the Rio Times Intelligence Desk. It carries the editor’s leader, the deep dive on Europe’s day of procedure and judgment, the country health check and the people who matter. Open the dossier · All Europe dossiers

Europe spent Wednesday morning settling accounts with two different pasts. Brussels proposed a procedure for attacks nobody claims, and The Hague sentenced four men for a war that ended in 1999.

Ursula von der Leyen asked the Union for a switch any capital could throw. A courtroom in the Netherlands closed a case that had run since April 2023.

Read across Dutch, Swedish, Italian and Ukrainian outlets in their English editions, the Dutch parliament’s own notice in Dutch and the French constitutional council’s decision in French. Read also across European and American wire reporting, court and central bank statements, and our own Europe desk.

Strasbourg Proposes A Switch Anyone Can Throw

Ursula von der Leyen delivered her State of the Union address in Strasbourg from shortly after 9 a.m. Strasbourg time. She proposed an Emergency Security Protocol for attacks that fall below the level of war.

She told the chamber it was time for Europe’s own Article 4, naming the NATO clause under which members consult when they feel threatened. Eunews carried that wording on 16 September 2026.

One member state could trigger the protocol, after which all twenty-seven governments would convene to coordinate a response, the security outlet The Record reported. She did not set out what follows once they have convened.

She listed cyberattacks, sabotage, arson and drone incursions, and said they were ramping up every day, in the account The Journal carried on 16 September 2026. The Record cited recent incidents in Denmark, Lithuania and Poland and an attempted drone attack in Leipzig.

She also proposed a European Security Council seating the United Kingdom, Norway, Canada and Ukraine alongside the twenty-seven. Agence France-Presse reported her saying the Commission would set out ideas to make it real.

Europe has raised defence spending by 80 per cent over five years, she said, in the account Euronews carried on 16 September 2026. A procedure costs less than a capability and arrives sooner.

The Rest Of The Speech Was An Invoice

The Union’s trade deficit with China now stands at one billion euros a day, she said, calling the pattern unsustainable. Eunews carried the figure on 16 September 2026.

She offered Canada the first associate membership in the Union’s history, with Prime Minister Mark Carney seated in the chamber. The accounts this desk read carry no description of what that status would contain, and all twenty-seven governments would have to agree.

On Russia she asked for enforcement of existing sanctions rather than new ones. Union ambassadors extended sanctions on nearly 3,000 people and entities by one week only, to 22 September 2026, after France and Slovakia withheld agreement.

Both governments want the businessman Alisher Usmanov removed from the list, Euronews reported on 14 September 2026. She asked for enforcement on a morning when enforcement had stalled.

She asked member states to accept new own resources, meaning revenue raised at Union level, for the 2028 to 2034 budget. Brussels Signal reported that Germany and other net contributors have resisted that idea.

Manfred Weber of the European People’s Party pressed for reform of the emissions trading system. Terry Reintke of the Greens demanded an inquiry committee into weak enforcement of the Green Deal, Brussels Signal reported. Jordan Bardella of Patriots for Europe demanded European preference in public procurement.

On the crossings at Ceuta she said, in the account The Journal carried: “Ceuta’s border is a European border. Because Ceuta is Spain. Ceuta is Europe.”

Italy reintroduced border controls with Spain over those crossings on 31 July 2026, Euronews reported. Rome extended them for a further fifteen days on 15 September 2026, and Spain imposed reciprocal controls.

She promised a heatwave plan after a summer in which 660,000 hectares burned and roughly 12 million tonnes of crops were lost. A list this long is a budget request written as prose.

The Hague Delivers A Sentence And Receives A Riot

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers began pronouncing judgment at 10 a.m. The Hague time, the hour carried in the day’s reporting. It convicted Hashim Thaçi and three co-defendants of war crimes.

Thaçi and Jakup Krasniqi received twenty-five years each, Kadri Veseli eighteen and Rexhep Selimi thirteen, all with credit for time already served. Prosecutors brought the four to The Hague on 4 and 5 November 2020.

The panel convicted them over the arbitrary detention of 385 people, the torture of 303, cruel treatment of 49 and the murder of 96. It acquitted all four of crimes against humanity.

Presiding Judge Charles Smith delivered the sentence, and Thaçi, who is 58, stood silently during sentencing and denies the charges. The court’s own statement names no appeal deadline.

Glauk Konjufca, Kosovo’s foreign minister, called it “a terrible, draconian verdict for Kosovo, for our war of liberation”, European Western Balkans reported. Thousands had gathered in Pristina in support of the four, and protesters outside the EULEX headquarters scuffled with riot police.

At the Malieveld in The Hague, demonstrators threw stones and flagpoles just after noon, and police used pepper spray, tear gas and a water cannon. Police arrested two people, and at least one officer was hurt.

The trial opened on 3 April 2023 and heard 134 witnesses in court. Nearly six years of detention produced one morning of sentences.

The Netherlands Finds Another Pipe

Contractors removed a pipe from the rails near Teuge, between Apeldoorn and Deventer, after services stopped at 9.30 p.m. Amsterdam time on 15 September 2026. Staff had taken a metal bar off the track between Holten and Rijssen that afternoon.

Mirjam van Velthuizen, ProRail’s chief executive, told the programme Nieuwsuur there was some camera footage but very little from the places where the incidents happened. She said the network would get more cameras and closer surveillance.

NL Times reported on 16 September 2026 that pipes and cables had been placed at more than thirty-five locations during Tuesday morning’s outage. The count reported on the day itself was about twenty.

Police arrested seven farmers, aged 25 to 70, over fires set on the A2 motorway near Breukelen on Budget Day. They were released after questioning and remain suspects.

Vincent Karremans, the infrastructure minister, said the acts made him angry and that he would press charges. This desk found no statement by the police or the prosecution service connecting the motorway fires to the rail sabotage.

Party leaders opened two days of debate on the budget at 10.15 a.m. Amsterdam time, with Prime Minister Rob Jetten due to answer on Thursday. His minority cabinet still needs ten votes in the lower house and sixteen in the senate.

The Kids Act Receives Its Numbers

Von der Leyen told the chamber there should be no social media below thirteen and no personal account below fifteen. CNN carried that wording on 16 September 2026.

The Commission presents the EU Kids Act on Thursday 17 September 2026, with Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen beside her. Agence Europe reported that date on 15 September 2026.

A draft circulating before the speech set four brackets: no access below three, parent-controlled accounts from three, introductory accounts from thirteen and independent accounts from fifteen. PPC Land described that text on 15 September 2026.

The same draft reaches video-sharing services, online games, chatbots and companion applications. Whether the published text matches it will be known on Thursday.

France’s Conseil constitutionnel struck down a national ban on accounts below fifteen in decision 2026-911 DC of 14 August 2026. It held that the legislature could not impose a general prohibition without disregarding the freedom of expression and communication. The proposal follows Australia’s ban on accounts for under-sixteens, ABC News in Australia reported.

The European Parliament and all twenty-seven governments must agree before any of it binds a platform. An announced age is not yet a law.

Stockholm Is Still Counting

Sweden voted on 13 September 2026 and has not finished counting. About 300,000 early and overseas ballots remained, The Local reported on 15 September 2026.

Anna Nyqvist, who heads the Election Authority’s administrative office, said an updated preliminary parliamentary result would not arrive before Thursday. The count of those late ballots began on Wednesday.

The authority’s own website states that the Riksdag result is expected to be finalised during the weekend after election day. Those are two separate dates for two separate things.

On the count reported on 15 September 2026 the four opposition parties held 176 seats against 173 for the governing bloc. The new Riksdag convenes on 28 September 2026.

The Rate Arrives Before The Answer

The European Central Bank’s deposit rate, the rate it pays banks on money left with it overnight, reached 2.50 per cent on 16 September 2026. The bank decided the rise on 10 September 2026, from 2.25 per cent.

It is the second increase of the cycle, the bank’s own record shows, with rates left unchanged in between, on 23 July 2026. The bank’s own projections put euro area inflation at 3.0 per cent this year, 2.5 per cent in 2027 and 2.1 per cent in 2028.

Christine Lagarde, the bank’s president, said it was not pre-committing to any particular path for rates. Those projections are the bank’s forecasts, and forecasts of this kind have been wrong before.

The bank’s own reference rate was US$1.1539 to the euro on 15 September 2026, published at around 4 p.m. Frankfurt time. Trading Economics attributed Wednesday’s softness in the euro to dollar strength before the American rate decision.

Brent crude settled at US$108.75 a barrel on 15 September 2026, against US$105.68 the day before. Investing.com’s futures series put Wednesday’s range at US$107.63 to US$108.59 while the session was open.

The United States Federal Reserve decides its own rate at 2 p.m. Washington time, after this edition closed. We do not know the outcome.

EU Perspectives read European gas storage at 65.4 per cent full on 1 September 2026, against 77.4 per cent a year earlier. A bank raising rates against an energy bill is answering a question it did not ask.

What This Means From Latin America

Brazil already regulates children’s accounts, and the rule Brussels proposes rhymes with it. Law 15,211 of 2025 links the account of any user under sixteen to a legal guardian.

Its grace period ended on 17 March 2026, and Brazil’s data protection authority enforces the law. This desk could not verify when administrative sanctions begin or the ceiling on fines.

The Commission’s circulating draft keeps a guardian in the loop up to fifteen, in four brackets from age three. Brazil and Brussels both make the guardian the gate, and differ on when it opens.

The Union’s interim trade agreement with Mercosur has applied provisionally since 1 May 2026, and the European Parliament has still to consent to the wider partnership. A budget argument in Strasbourg is therefore also a South American file.

Exactly a year ago, on 16 September 2025, Colombia’s Special Jurisdiction for Peace sentenced seven former guerrilla commanders to eight years of restorative work. The Hague answered a comparable question on Wednesday with twenty-five years in a cell.

For a reader in São Paulo or Bogotá the day offers a login screen, a tariff schedule and a mirror. Two continents asked the same question this morning and answered it at different lengths.

What We Are Watching

The EU Kids Act on Thursday — whether the published text carries the thresholds of thirteen and fifteen that Ursula von der Leyen named, and how it treats games and chatbots.

— whether the published text carries the thresholds of thirteen and fifteen that Ursula von der Leyen named, and how it treats games and chatbots. The Emergency Security Protocol — whether the Commission publishes a legal text, and what it says happens after the twenty-seven have convened.

— whether the Commission publishes a legal text, and what it says happens after the twenty-seven have convened. Sweden’s ballots — the updated preliminary parliamentary result due on Thursday, and the final count the Election Authority expects during the following weekend.

— the updated preliminary parliamentary result due on Thursday, and the final count the Election Authority expects during the following weekend. The Dutch debate — whether Rob Jetten answers on Thursday with ten lower-house votes and sixteen senators in hand.

— whether Rob Jetten answers on Thursday with ten lower-house votes and sixteen senators in hand. The Dutch track — whether the national police name a suspect or a motive for the pipes found on Tuesday and again on Tuesday night.

— whether the national police name a suspect or a motive for the pipes found on Tuesday and again on Tuesday night. Sanctions on 22 September 2026 — whether France and Slovakia still withhold agreement over the listing of Alisher Usmanov.

— whether France and Slovakia still withhold agreement over the listing of Alisher Usmanov. Mark Carney in Strasbourg — what the Canadian prime minister says to the European Parliament on Thursday about an associate membership nobody has defined.

The Bigger Picture What this desk does not know is most of what matters underneath Wednesday. This desk found no published investigative finding on who flew the drone destroyed over Lithuania on 15 September 2026, nor on what it carried. Nor could the desk establish who placed the pipes on Dutch track, or whether Denmark’s summoned Russian ambassador has met anyone. We asked no minister directly, and we are not treating silence as a denial. The Kosovo Specialist Chambers took from November 2020, when the four arrived in The Hague, to September 2026. Courts of this kind measure their work in presidential terms, not news cycles. Europe’s answer to unclaimed attacks has moved from statements to procedure inside a week. A procedure is what an alliance builds when attribution keeps arriving late. Each of Wednesday’s files is a form of bookkeeping: a court settling 1999, a bank settling this year’s energy bill, a parliament arguing over 2028. Europe is paying, in order, for things it has already done.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Ursula von der Leyen propose on 16 September 2026?

She proposed an Emergency Security Protocol, which one member state could trigger to convene all twenty-seven and coordinate a response to sabotage, arson, cyberattacks or drone incursions. She also proposed a European Security Council seating the United Kingdom, Norway, Canada and Ukraine.

What did the court in The Hague decide about Hashim Thaçi?

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers convicted him and three co-defendants of war crimes and sentenced him to twenty-five years, with credit for time already served. It acquitted all four of crimes against humanity.

When do the European Union’s rules on children’s accounts appear?

The Commission presents the EU Kids Act on Thursday 17 September 2026. The European Parliament and all twenty-seven governments must then agree before it binds any platform.

What changes now the European Central Bank’s deposit rate is 2.50 per cent?

Banks earn more on money left with the central bank overnight, which over time lifts what savers and borrowers pay and receive. Christine Lagarde said the bank is not pre-committing to any particular path from here.

Sources in English: the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the European Central Bank, the Swedish Election Authority and the Dutch lower house. Speech reporting from Euronews, Eunews, The Record, The Journal, Agence France-Presse via the Kyiv Post, ABC News, CNN and Brussels Signal. The verdict via NPR, Al Jazeera and European Western Balkans. Dutch reporting from NL Times and DutchNews.nl, Swedish from The Local, and the children’s draft from PPC Land and Agence Europe. The French decision is Conseil constitutionnel decision 2026-911 DC of 14 August 2026, read in French. Market figures from Investing.com and Trading Economics; storage from EU Perspectives · 1–16 September 2026.

World.title: Ethiopia Harvest May Fall 30% as Kiremt Rains Fail
World.content:
ETHIOPIA · FOOD SECURITY

Key Facts — What is the meher Ethiopia’s main harvest, fed by the kiremt rains of June to September. It produces more than 85% of the country’s crops.

— What has gone wrong The kiremt rains failed across much of the country. Cumulative rainfall ranks among the driest on record.

— How bad The famine early warning network FEWS NET says the meher harvest could be up to 30% below average nationally.

— Why A strong El Niño. The US Climate Prediction Center has had an El Niño advisory in force since September, with the tropical Pacific 1.8 degrees above normal in August.

— Who is worst affected Tigray, eastern Amhara, Afar and eastern Oromia. Some lowland areas may see little or no meher production at all.

— Where it stands now Crisis-level food insecurity is widespread and expected to persist into January 2027.

Ethiopia grows most of its food in one harvest. This year the rains that feed it did not come.

FEWS NET says Ethiopia’s meher harvest could come in up to 30% below average.

Ethiopia’s main meher harvest could be up to 30% below average nationally, according to FEWS NET. The kiremt rains that feed it were among the poorest on record. A strong El Niño is under way in the Pacific.

One Harvest, Most of the Food

The kiremt rains run from June to September and feed the meher harvest, gathered from October.

FEWS NET puts the meher at over 85% of Ethiopia’s domestic crop production.

A second, smaller season called belg supplies the rest, mostly in the south and east.

When kiremt fails there is no second chance within the same year.

What the Rains Did

Rainfall was far below average across northern, eastern and central Ethiopia through the season.

FEWS NET’s August update, with data to 27 August, found deficits exceeding 50% of average across much of the country.

Cumulative seasonal rainfall ranks among the driest on record for most of Ethiopia.

Planting was delayed and maize and sorghum, the staples of the affected areas, are the crops most exposed.

The El Niño Behind It

The US Climate Prediction Center issued an El Niño advisory on 10 September 2026.

Sea surface temperatures in the central-eastern Pacific reached 1.8 degrees Celsius above normal in August.

The centre gives better than a 90% chance of a very strong event through the northern winter. It puts the chance of one exceeding any El Niño since 1950 at 75%.

The World Meteorological Organization puts the probability of continued El Niño conditions through early 2027 at effectively 100%. A return to neutral or La Niña is not anticipated.

Why El Niño Dries the Ethiopian Highlands

El Niño shifts rainfall patterns across the tropics, and in the Horn of Africa it typically suppresses the June to September rains.

The same event usually brings heavier rains to the region between October and December, which falls after the meher is already lost.

Ethiopia’s 2015 and 2016 drought, one of its worst in decades, followed the same pattern.

That is why a Pacific temperature reading matters to a farmer in Amhara.

Cumulative kiremt rainfall ranks among the driest on record for most of Ethiopia.

Where It Is Worst

FEWS NET’s East Africa seasonal monitor of 11 September confirms below-average meher production for Tigray, eastern Amhara, Afar and eastern Oromia.

Some lowland areas may produce little or no meher crop at all.

The effect crosses the border. Kenyan maize production is running about 28% below average nationally and 43% below in the North Rift.

Ethiopia’s own meteorology institute forecast a poor season in May, so the outcome was anticipated.

A short harvest raises cereal prices from October, when a normal year would lower them.

What It Means for Prices and Hunger

Crisis-level food insecurity is already widespread and is expected to persist into January 2027.

FEWS NET reports 2.45 million people in Tigray alone needing emergency food assistance.

Ethiopian headline inflation was 15.3% in July 2026, which erodes purchasing power before any harvest shortfall reaches the market.

A short harvest raises cereal prices from October, which is exactly when a normal year would bring them down.

What Could Soften It

Ethiopia has expanded irrigated wheat production substantially, which is not dependent on kiremt rainfall.

The October to December rains are forecast to be enhanced. That helps pasture, livestock and belg planting, though it comes too late for the meher.

Government and humanitarian agencies have a functioning early warning system and knew this was coming from May.

None of that replaces 30% of a national harvest.

What to Watch

The harvest assessment from October, which converts a forecast into a measured shortfall.

Cereal prices in Ethiopian markets, the fastest indicator of whether the shortfall is biting.

The October to December rains, which determine whether livestock recover.

And humanitarian funding, which in a year like this decides how a shortfall translates into hunger.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How bad is Ethiopia’s harvest this year?

FEWS NET says the meher harvest could be up to 30% below average nationally. Some lowland areas may see little or no production.

What is the meher?

Ethiopia’s main harvest, fed by the June to September kiremt rains. It provides more than 85% of domestic crop production.

Is there really an El Niño?

Yes. The US Climate Prediction Center issued an El Niño advisory on 10 September 2026. The Pacific ran 1.8 degrees above normal in August.

Which areas are worst affected?

Tigray, eastern Amhara, Afar and eastern Oromia, according to FEWS NET’s 11 September seasonal monitor.

How many people need help?

Crisis-level food insecurity is widespread into January 2027, with 2.45 million people in Tigray needing emergency food assistance.

Does this affect neighbouring countries?

Yes. Kenyan maize production is running about 28% below average nationally and 43% below in the North Rift.

Sources: FEWS NET Ethiopia Food Security Outlook Update (August 2026) and East Africa Seasonal Monitor (11 September 2026), NOAA Climate Prediction Center, World Meteorological Organization, Ethiopian Meteorology Institute.

World.title: Morocco Election 2026: Where the Minimum Wage Stands
World.content:
MOROCCO · ELECTION

Key Facts — When Moroccans vote 23 September 2026, for 395 seats in the House of Representatives.

— The electorate 15.8 million registered voters, 7,288 candidates on 1,850 lists.

— The minimum wage now MAD 3,422 a month in the private sector from January 2026, about US$361. The agricultural minimum is MAD 2,533, roughly US$267.

— What parties are promising A 15% rise from the Party of Progress and Socialism. The left alliance proposes a unified net minimum of MAD 5,000, about US$527, by 2029.

— The youth problem Voters aged 18 to 24 are about 3% of the register. Under-35s are 18%, while voters over 60 are 30%.

— The unemployment figure to get right Youth unemployment was 27.2% in the second quarter of 2026, on a new survey. The widely quoted 37.2% is the 2025 figure on the old one.

Moroccan parties are competing on the minimum wage. The voters it would most affect are barely on the electoral register.

Morocco votes on 23 September 2026 for 395 seats in the House of Representatives.

Morocco votes on 23 September 2026 in a legislative election where the minimum wage has become a central promise. Voters aged 18 to 24 make up about 3% of the electoral register.

The Election

The House of Representatives has 395 seats: 305 from local constituencies and 90 from regional lists reserved for women.

A majority requires 198 seats. No Moroccan party has come close to one in the multi-party era.

There are 15.8 million registered voters and 7,288 candidates across 1,850 lists.

The state has allocated MAD 450 million in public campaign funding, about US$47.5 million. Of that, MAD 50 million, about US$5.3 million, is reserved for lists headed by candidates aged 35 or under.

Where the Minimum Wage Stands

The private-sector minimum, the SMIG, rose to MAD 3,422.72 a month in January 2026, about US$361.

It is calculated as MAD 17.92 an hour, about US$1.89, over 191 hours, up from MAD 17.10. The instrument is decree 2.25.983.

The agricultural minimum, the SMAG, rose to MAD 2,533.44 in April 2026, roughly US$267, at MAD 97.44 a day over 26 days.

Both are the second instalment of a tripartite social accord signed in April 2024. The SMIG has risen nearly 20% since 2021 and the SMAG nearly 25%.

What the Parties Are Offering

The Party of Progress and Socialism proposes a 15% rise covering both minimums, in two stages in 2027 and 2030.

It also proposes a minimum dignity income of MAD 1,000, about US$105, for households in multidimensional poverty. Its jobs pledge is one million net jobs over five years.

The left alliance joins the Federation of the Democratic Left and the Unified Socialist Party. It proposes a single unified minimum of MAD 5,000 net by 2029, roughly US$527.

Its path runs MAD 4,100 in 2027, about US$432, then MAD 4,550 in 2028, some US$480, then MAD 5,000 in 2029.

The Number Everyone Is Quoting Wrong

Youth unemployment among 15 to 24-year-olds is widely given as 37.2% for 2026. That figure is from 2025.

Morocco’s statistics agency, the High Commission for Planning, put it at 27.2% in the second quarter of 2026. That was down from 29.2% in the first.

Overall unemployment was 9.5% in the same quarter, down from 10.8%.

The agency changed its survey methodology in 2026 and says comparison with the old series is not possible. A government revising its own labour figures downward in an election year is itself part of the story.

Voters aged 18 to 24 are about 3% of Morocco’s electoral register.

Who Is On the Register

Voters aged 18 to 24 are about 3% of the 15.8 million registered, some sources rounding to 4%.

That is roughly 474,000 people out of a potential cohort near 3.9 million.

Adding 25 to 34-year-olds brings the under-35 share to 18%. Voters over 60 are 30%.

Low youth registration long predates the current wage promises, so it measures enrolment rather than a verdict on any policy.

The Group Nobody Reaches

A joint study counted 2.9 million Moroccans aged 15 to 29 not in employment, education or training. It was produced by the High Commission for Planning with the International Labour Organization and the European Union.

It was presented in Rabat on 14 April 2026 and puts the share at roughly one in three.

That population is larger than the entire 18 to 24 electoral roll.

A minimum wage rise reaches them only if they are working. That is the gap the promises do not close.

Much Moroccan employment is informal, where the legal minimum does not apply.

What a Moroccan Minimum Wage Buys

MAD 3,422 a month is about US$361, in a country where Casablanca rents and food prices have risen faster than wages.

The formal private sector is where the SMIG applies. Much Moroccan employment is informal, where it does not.

Agriculture, where the lower SMAG applies, employs around a third of Moroccan workers.

Raising the legal minimum lifts those inside the formal sector and leaves those outside it where they were.

What to Watch

Turnout on 23 September, and the age profile of who actually votes.

Whether either wage pledge survives coalition negotiation, since no party will govern alone.

The next quarterly labour figures, which will show whether the improvement holds.

And the 2027 instalment of the social accord, which is the next scheduled wage decision regardless of who wins.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does Morocco vote?

23 September 2026, for 395 seats in the House of Representatives.

What is Morocco’s minimum wage?

MAD 3,422.72 a month in the private sector from January 2026, about US$361. Agriculture is MAD 2,533.44, roughly US$267.

What are parties promising?

The Party of Progress and Socialism proposes a 15% rise in two stages. The left alliance proposes a unified MAD 5,000 net, about US$527, by 2029.

What is youth unemployment?

27.2% among 15 to 24-year-olds in the second quarter of 2026. The 37.2% figure often quoted is from 2025 under a different survey.

How many young people are registered to vote?

Voters aged 18 to 24 are about 3% of the register. Under-35s are 18%, and over-60s are 30%.

How much public campaign funding is there?

MAD 450 million, about US$47.5 million. Of that, MAD 50 million, some US$5.3 million, goes to lists led by candidates aged 35 or under.

Sources: Haut-Commissariat au Plan, Médias24, La Quotidienne, Morocco World News, Bulletin Officiel, International Labour Organization.

World.title: Cape Verde President Neves Seeks a Second Term
World.content:
CAPE VERDE · ELECTION

Key Facts — What happened President José Maria Neves announced on 14 September 2026 in Praia that he will seek a second term.

— When the vote is 15 November 2026.

— Who he is President since 2021, and before that prime minister from 2001 to 2016. He is the longest-serving head of government in the country’s democratic history.

— Who is standing in Janira Hopffer Almada, president of the National Assembly, takes over as interim head of state. She is the first woman ever to hold the office.

— Who else is running Janine Lélis, minister of state for defence and territorial cohesion, and Joana Rosa, minister of justice.

— What changed this year His own party won the May parliamentary election, so the cohabitation that defined his first term has ended.

Cape Verde’s president stepped aside on Monday to run for re-election. A woman is running the country in the meantime, for the first time.

President José Maria Neves announced his candidacy for a second term in Praia on 14 September 2026.

President José Maria Neves announced in Praia on 14 September 2026 that he will seek a second term. Cape Verde votes on 15 November.

The Announcement

Neves declared in Praia on Monday 14 September. He said he was announcing his candidature for a second mandate as President of the Republic of Cabo Verde.

He would put the experience he has gained at the service of the future, he said. The aim, in his words, is a victorious and prosperous nation.

His campaign team includes Mário Lúcio Sousa as national campaign manager, with Lúcia Fortes on women’s outreach and Viviane Brito on youth.

The African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde, which he once led, formally endorsed his re-candidacy the following day.

A Woman Runs the Country

Cape Verdean presidents suspend their mandate when they campaign, and Neves did so immediately.

Janira Hopffer Almada, elected president of the National Assembly on 18 June 2026, takes over as interim head of state.

She is the first woman ever to hold the Cape Verdean presidency, even on an interim basis.

She will hold it until the November result is declared.

Who He Is

Neves was prime minister from 2001 to 2016, across three terms.

He won the presidency in 2021 in the first round, with just over 51%.

Cape Verdean presidents cannot formally belong to a party while in office, though parties endorse them. His own background is in the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde.

The office is largely ceremonial, with reserve powers over dissolution and the promulgation of laws.

The Cohabitation Ended in May

For most of his term Neves faced a government from the rival Movement for Democracy, an arrangement Cape Verdeans call cohabitation.

That ended on 17 May 2026, when his own party won 37 of the 72 parliamentary seats.

The Movement for Democracy fell from 38 seats to 33, and Francisco Carvalho replaced Ulisses Correia e Silva as prime minister.

Neves is therefore running as an incumbent aligned with the government rather than as a counterweight to it.

The Field

Two ministers from the outgoing administration have declared against him.

Janine Lélis has been minister of state for defence and territorial cohesion since 2021.

Joana Rosa has been minister of justice over the same period.

Neves faces no serious challenge from within his own camp.

Cape Verde has held competitive elections since 1991.

Why the Presidency Matters Here

Cape Verde is a ten-island archipelago of around half a million people, 570 kilometres off the West African coast.

It has held peaceful, competitive elections since 1991 and ranks among Africa’s most stable democracies.

The president is the guarantor of the constitution and the arbiter when parliament and government disagree.

With one party now holding both the presidency and the government, that arbitration role becomes less contested and, to some, less necessary.

Cape Verde depends on tourism, remittances, fisheries and external financing.

What the Country Runs On

Tourism, remittances from a diaspora larger than the resident population, fisheries and external financing.

It imports most of what it eats and all of its fuel, which makes it acutely exposed to shipping and energy prices.

Its strategic position in the mid-Atlantic has drawn security and infrastructure interest from Europe, the United States and China.

Whoever wins in November inherits those same constraints, because the presidency does not set economic policy.

What to Watch

Whether further candidates declare before nominations close.

Whether Neves wins in the first round, as he did in 2021.

Turnout, which in Cape Verdean presidential elections has run well below parliamentary turnout.

And how Janira Hopffer Almada’s interim tenure is received, since it is a first for the country.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is running for president of Cape Verde?

Incumbent José Maria Neves, who declared on 14 September 2026, along with ministers Janine Lélis and Joana Rosa.

When is the election?

15 November 2026.

Who is acting president?

Janira Hopffer Almada, president of the National Assembly, the first woman ever to hold the office in Cape Verde.

Why is there an acting president?

Cape Verdean presidents suspend their mandate while campaigning. Neves did so on declaring.

Has the political balance changed?

Yes. The African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde won 37 of 72 seats in May 2026. That ended the cohabitation of Neves’s first term.

How powerful is the presidency?

Largely ceremonial, with reserve powers over dissolution and the promulgation of laws.

Sources: Expresso das Ilhas, Africanews, Assembleia Nacional de Cabo Verde, Comissão Nacional de Eleições.

World.title: Mali Jails Journalist Two Years Over Kidal Remark
World.content:
MALI · PRESS FREEDOM

Key Facts — Who was jailed Abdrahamane Keïta, publication director of the Malian newspaper Le Témoin. Some outlets spell his first name Abderhamane.

— The sentence Two years in prison without suspension, plus one million CFA francs in damages to the state, about US$1,760.

— When 14 September 2026, according to AFP and the Committee to Protect Journalists. He was arrested on 9 June.

— Which court The Pôle national de lutte contre la cybercriminalité in Bamako, the national anti-cybercrime unit, which both investigated and tried him.

— What he said On a television debate programme he described the town of Kidal as being run by the leader of the armed group JNIM. Accounts of his exact words differ.

— What happens next His lawyers announced an appeal at the verdict.

A Malian editor said on television that an armed group runs a town in the north. A cybercrime court gave him two years.

A Bamako court sentenced the editor of Le Témoin to two years on 14 September 2026.
