World.content: Tickets to the festival happening on 26 and 27 of February went on sale back in April. Over 30,000 tickets were sold in an hour without a line-up even on the cards at that stage. Another 15,000 had been held back for Thursday’s announcement.

World.title: Uncosted MMP referendum: Could Māori seats be on the chopping block?
World.content:
The government does not know how much an MMP referendum might cost, and National's leader is refusing to rule out a question on abolishing the Māori seats.

The ACT Party proposed such a question for the last referendum on MMP in 2011 at select committee, but it was prevented by National's confidence and supply agreement with the then-Māori Party.

After Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's on-air musings about MMP early last month became an election promise to hold a referendum on the electoral system, surprising his National Party caucus, RNZ sought further details about how it would work and what it might cost.

Neither the Ministry of Justice nor the Electoral Commission could give RNZ a ballpark estimate for what a referendum might cost.

A spokesperson for the Electoral Commission, which would likely run the referendum, said "we can't provide a ballpark cost for a referendum as it depends on costs at the time".

The Commission said factors affecting potential costs would include whether a referendum was being held alongside a general election, as a standalone poll or by postal vote.

They pointed to about $25 million having been set aside by the Ministry of Justice for the proposed referendum for a four-year term, which the coalition toyed with but ultimately abandoned work on ahead of the election.

A cabinet paper put the costs of the four-year-term referendum at more like $27m, including $9.21m for a public information campaign.

"The budget would have included operational costs for conduct of the referendum by the Electoral Commission and a public information campaign about the subject of the referendum by the Ministry of Justice," the Commission said.

The Ministry itself similarly was "not able to supply a 'ballpark' figure for the cost of running various referenda", and also highlighted the estimated cost of the four-year-term poll which would have run alongside the 2026 election.

The last referendums held outside an election were on changing the flag, in 2015 and 2016. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

That breaks down to $18.7m for the Commission to run the referendum, and $6.2m for an accompanying information campaign.

"We do not have cost estimates/historic costs for holding an in-person voting referendum outside of a general election," the ministry said.

When Luxon initially committed to the referendum on Newstalk ZB, he had been asked if he would "do that if you were prime minister next year".

RNZ questioned him about whether that meant the referendum would be held in 2027 or if he was prime minister next year, and whether - given ACT's previous stance on the referendum - he could rule out a question on the Māori seats.

"Sorry, look, again, you'll see all our constitutional policy as part of a justice policy that will get released closer to the election," he said.

The Prime Minister's office has ignored multiple requests from RNZ over the past month seeking clarity on those matters.

Parliament's library confirmed the last referenda held in New Zealand during an election were in 2020 on the End of Life Choice Act and Cannabis Legalisation, at a combined cost of $12.9m - some $5.5m under budget. The separate cost of running the election that year was $99.9m.

The Justice Ministry confirmed the last referendums held outside an election were on changing the flag, in 2015 and 2016.

World.title: 'Chilling': Business groups speak out against National's supermarket break-up plan
World.content:
Pak'nSave Tauranga owner responds to National’s new policy Morning Report Download MP3 6m

National's push to drive competition in the supermarket sector by breaking up one of the key players has drawn stinging criticism from the country's leading business groups.

And one Pak'nSave owner says it could even see prices rise.

National, if re-elected, says it would legislate to split up the Kiwi-owned Foodstuffs, although only after the Commerce Commission investigated to make sure it would benefit consumers.

Dean Waddell, owner of Pak'nSave Tauranga and chairperson of Foodstuffs North Island, told Morning Report National's proposal would drive prices up.

He said Foodstuff was "gutted and concerned" by the proposal.

" We've spent a lot of time educating political parties around our co-operative structure," he said.

"We started with five co-ops, we're down to two and that's given us the scale and efficiencies and the buying power to stay competitive for our customers. So going back the other way and demerging for us just puts our member stores into a more higher-cost base and a potentially more uncompetitive situation in the years to come."

Despite Foodstuffs and Woolworths having between them more than 80 percent of the market, he disputed they were a duopoly - saying Foodstuffs was actually "a combination of 500 independent businesses" which work together to achieve efficiencies of scale.

"Don't forget it reduces our buying power as well, and we're still a relatively small business from a global scale."

He disputed claims independent Foodstuffs stores were avoiding competition with each other.

"We compete, you know, every day with our own sister members because, you know, that is how we're, that's in our DNA. We want to have more customers in our own stores to drive our own revenue."

Undermines reputation - BusinessNZ

BusinessNZ likened the proposal to Labour's offshore ban on oil and gas exploration, which critics claimed had a chilling effect on investment.

Director of advocacy Catherine Beard described the move as alarming.

"This is a very concerning move by the National Party and sends a chilling signal to businesses across New Zealand that the Government can break up businesses. It also sends the wrong signal to foreign investors looking to invest in New Zealand. We consider this to be in the same league as Labour's ban on oil and gas exploration and New Zealand First's promise to split up the gentailers."

Beard said New Zealand had a strong reputation for predictable policy settings and National's move flew in the face of that.

"New Zealand has long benefited from a reputation for regulatory stability, respect for property rights and predictable policy settings. Measures of this nature risk undermining that reputation at a time when New Zealand needs investment, productivity growth and economic confidence."

Beard said while boosting competition in New Zealand's grocery sector was a worthwhile goal, interventions like these raised questions about whether it would deliver lower prices.

"Breaking businesses apart does not automatically create more competition, and it certainly does not guarantee cheaper groceries. Supermarkets rely heavily on scale across purchasing, distribution, logistics, technology and other infrastructure. If structural separation reduces those efficiencies or duplicates costs, there is a risk that some of those costs ultimately find their way to consumers."

Meanwhile, the Employers and Manufacturers Association was also critical. Head of advocacy Alan McDonald said the policy undermined the foundations of business and private property rights.

"Seeing a right-of-centre, business-focused political party like National suggest this type of policy will sit uneasily with businesses in New Zealand. It might be a populist policy for a grumpy electorate, but that doesn't make it a good policy."

McDonald agreed it sent a bad signal to investors.

World.title: Margaret Green sentenced for Manurewa manslaughter of partner Selwyn Robson
World.content:
A woman who fatally stabbed her partner in the neck with a serrated kitchen knife, in front of his young son, has been allowed a reduced prison sentence due in part to her history as a victim of severe domestic abuse.

But there was not enough evidence to suggest the stab victim, whom she had been dating for five months, was among those who had previously subjected her to sustained violence, a judge has noted.

Jurors in the High Court at Auckland found Margaret Jovander Green, 33, guilty of manslaughter in July after a three-week trial in which the Crown sought a murder conviction.

Green declined to testify during her trial and has said she has no memory of what happened.

But she was not acting in self-defence when she stabbed partner Selwyn Robson, 30, Justice James MacGillivray said.

She stabbed him with such force in the neck that the 20cm serrated blade penetrated his lung.

Green's lawyers suggested that, to a degree, the lack of self-defence was beside the point, and the judge agreed.

"While Ms Green stands here as an offender, she was undoubtedly a victim first," defence lawyer Susan Giles said, noting that her client's significant childhood trauma was compounded by "repeated intimate partner violence" as an adult.

It resulted in a situation, Giles said, in which "trauma is laid upon trauma until the person becomes so psychologically damaged that their responses are not driven by rational choice but by deeply ingrained survival mechanisms".

Deadly argument

The couple had been living together at a Manurewa sleepout in May last year when the stabbing occurred.

Neighbour Anthony Hepi testified at the trial that he was doing some washing that day when he heard arguing coming from the backyard.

Moments later, Hepi told jurors, Robson came running with blood "p***ing out of his neck".

"Some b**** stabbed me," he recalled the victim yelling.

Selwyn Robson was stabbed to death by his partner, who was convicted of manslaughter. NZME

Robson died at the scene. An autopsy revealed the knife went more than 9cm into his neck, damaging multiple blood vessels and causing major blood loss.

Justice MacGillivray said there was evidence at trial that the two had a "loving relationship", although they argued at times, and there was evidence that Robson had been violent on at least one occasion two months earlier.

On that occasion, Green had sent texts to a friend noting that Robson had given her a black eye.

But when the friend expressed distress over the revelation, Green told her to calm down, explaining she had been attacking Robson when he head-butted her rather than hitting her with a closed fist.

Another witness at trial said Robson had been violent towards her in the past.

On the morning of the stabbing, the two clearly got into an argument but it was not clear what it was about, the judge said.

Green told some witnesses she had become angry because Robson was talking down to her. She told another she had objected to her partner expecting her to watch his toddler son.

Green's accounts to witnesses about what happened next varied from Robson approaching her, to him kicking her in the face, to both hitting each other.

The argument was violent, but the judge said he was unsure to what extent.

A homicide investigation was launched after the death of Selwyn Robson in Manurewa. NZME

"The jury's rejection of self-defence shows that you were not facing a level of violence that justified the use of the knife," the judge said.

"Using the knife against Mr Robson was excessive and unjustified."

But the jury's verdict, after three days of deliberations, also made it clear that Green did not intend to cause death or appreciate that it might occur.

To make sense of what occurred, the judge said, it was important to consider her history and mental health at the time of the crime.

A report prepared for the court before sentencing said Green suffered an "unsettled childhood" that included physical and emotional abuse when she was put into state care aged nine.

Her mother introduced her to cannabis at age 12 and methamphetamine at 13, the court was told.

She was later expelled from school and, at 17, her mother introduced her to escort work.

As an adult, she was in a number of relationships in which she was regularly subjected to violence and suffered serious injuries, the judge noted.

In 2018, she was hospitalised with a traumatic brain injury during one such toxic long-term relationship.

The past abuse caused complex post-traumatic stress disorder, which a psychiatrist explained can result in difficulty regulating emotional responses to situations, as well as reactive and impulsive behaviour.

AUT lecturer Rachel Smith, an expert on family violence and trauma, noted women in situations such as Green's may respond to isolated incidents as if responding to the cumulative experience of past violence.

Justice MacGillivray rejected the defence suggestion that the homicide was an example of "excessive self-defence".

But he did agree Green lashed out at her partner in a dysregulated and impulsive act caused by PTSD and the "cumulative experiences of past violence" against her.

"There is no evidential foundation for concluding your relationship with Mr Robson was one of coercive control," he said.

Grief, forgiveness

Robson was remembered by his large family this week as someone with a wicked, sometimes dark sense of humour, an interest in passing on family heritage to the younger generation and a hard worker who prioritised looking after those he loved.

He was a Black Power member, but the patch didn't define him, multiple family members said in a series of victim impact statements.

Prosecutors also said there had been no evidence his gang membership had any bearing on the relationship.

"I carry grief, confusion and heaviness that does not go away," the victim's father, Patrick Robson, told the judge as Green stared ahead.

"I take no joy in seeing another person's life ruined, so I'm choosing to process this with ... humility. She has a family, and I do not wish further harm on them."

But the pain of losing his son is enduring, he said.

"This tragedy has shattered our family in ways that will continue to affect us for the rest of our lives," he said.

Green also refused to look as Wepiha Webster, one of the victim's nine siblings, offered his reluctant forgiveness.

"Forgiveness is a big word, one that you honestly don't deserve, but if I carry this hate it will eat me," he said. "I forgive you, not for you, but for my brother."

Another sibling, Arnold Robson, described his brother as someone who was "very staunch" but humble and always "whānau-oriented".

"He was so much more than the circumstances of his death," he said, adding he hoped his brother could be remembered "with love, with respect and as the person he truly was to us".

"His life mattered to me," he said. "His life mattered to our whānau."

New Zealand's enduring violence

At the sentencing hearing, Crown prosecutor Aysser Al-Janabi wished to distinguish Green's offending from cases in which female defendants felt trapped by lengthy relationships that involved significant degrees of domestic violence.

Green's "highly dysfunctional" relationship with Robson was short and it involved at least one other scenario before he died in which he was the victim, Al-Janabi said, explaining there was no evidence of Green suffering social control, financial control or isolation.

The Crown suggested a 10 percent reduction for her background and 10 percent for her rejected offer to plead guilty to manslaughter six weeks before the murder trial began, but no discounts for remorse or rehab efforts.

Justice MacGillivray ordered a starting point of four years and three months' imprisonment before allowing 20 percent in combined discounts for her background, remorse and efforts at rehabilitation. Another 15 percent was allowed for her earlier offer to plead guilty.

Justice James MacGillivray. NZME / Michael Craig

It resulted in a sentence of two years and nine months' imprisonment.

Green's lawyers assured the court she is remorseful for having killed "her best friend and the love of her life".

"Her complex PTSD has deprived her of the ability to fully remember or comprehend what occurred in those moments," Giles said. "The fragments of memory that she is able to retrieve are, in her own description, akin to awakening in a nightmare."

But she has begun working with ACC counsellors and psychiatrists to understand how lifelong trauma has shaped her responses and behaviour, the defence lawyer said.

"Ms Green's actions on that day were a culmination of a lifetime of experiences that reflect the enduring complexity of family violence in New Zealand," she said.

"This requires the court to confront the consequences of what happens when children slip through the cracks, when they are exposed to multifaceted childhood abuse, abandoned by those who should protect them and denied the stable and supportive foundation necessary to become healthy adults."

Where to get help:

If it is an emergency and you feel like you or someone else is at risk, call 111.

Family Violence

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: New charter school given approval to become one of NZ's biggest schools
World.content:
* This article has been updated as the amount of government funding is in dispute

An online charter school that opened just nine months ago already has permission to become one of the country's biggest schools.

Aotearoa Infinite Academy opened at the start of this year with 200 students, and has approval to grow to 2000 next year and 3000 in 2028.

The secondary school's growth is significant because other charter schools have remained relatively small, with the largest enrolling about 150 students.

A roll of 2000 would make the academy one of the 30 largest schools - and 3000 would put it in the top three to five, with government funding running to more than $20m a year.

For comparison, last year Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu (the Correspondence School) had 10,349 students, Rangitoto College 4081, Mt Albert Grammar 3576, Macleans College 2981, while Avondale College, Westlake Boys High and Auckland Grammar School all had more than 2700.

A Charter School Agency document said a secondary charter school of 1005 students would receive $10,741 for each student, and with 2500 students, per-student funding would be $8892.

However, the academy said it was funded at a rate of $13,560 per student for the first 200 students, and $6983 per student beyond 200.

The academy's website said it offered online classes with about 20 students each, teaching the Pearson private curriculum during years 9-11, and NCEA during years 12 and 13.

Earlier this year, the school said it had grown to 450 students after just six weeks, with permission to grow to 600 in term two this year.

RNZ asked the Charter School Agency about the school's growth and what independent monitoring of the school had been conducted to ensure it warranted expansion.

The agency said it recently approved an application to increase the school's roll to 2000 next year and 3000 in 2028, but did not cite any independent checking.

"This approval was based on evidence of growing demand, and satisfactory results against the attendance and achievement performance targets," it said.

"AIA were required to demonstrate how the school would manage a larger roll, including bringing on additional staff, supporting new students and meeting increased demand for in-person exam facilities.

"As with all charter schools, we will continue to monitor the school's performance against its contract. This includes targets for roll numbers, student attendance, and achievement. In contrast to state schools, the funding AIA receives is dependent on it continuing to meet these requirements."

The academy was owned by Crimson Consulting, where former National Party leader and Prime Minister Sir John Key was a director, and was part of the Crimson Academies Group which included private online schools the Crimson Global Academy and Mount Hobson Academy, as well as Future School, a private school in Auckland.

Academy principal Saira Boyle told RNZ the school's enrolments came from a range of backgrounds and areas, though a large number were from the Auckland region.

"We've got students who've come from the public school system, some who've come from the private school system, some from homeschooling."

Boyle said daily attendance was at 90 percent or more, and more than half of the school's students were attending more than 90 percent of their classes - the benchmark for regular attendance.

She said the school had 600 students, with about 400 more on a waitlist. Student achievement was also good.

"We have a large number of students, a significant number in reading, writing and maths who are at or above where they need to be. We're also supporting students who need that extra little bit of a boost with a range of intervention classes," she said.

Asked if the school should have been subject to independent monitoring before gaining approval for significant growth, Boyle said the school could be trusted.

"We are sending regular reports into the Charter School Agency and I feel really, really confident that the powers that be see the good that we are doing. They can see how we're operating and they feel confident enough to give us that roll increase," she said.

The PPTA's president Chris Abercombie said he was concerned about such rapid growth at a school. RNZ / Angus Dreaver

Post Primary Teachers' Association president Chris Abercrombie said there should be more publicly-available data about the school.

"At the moment we don't know if they're doing a good job or a great job or a bad job, yet they've been allowed to increase by 1500 students roughly in the space of two years."

Abercrombie said he was concerned about such rapid growth, because it was difficult to manage.

He said those concerns were amplified for an online school, which needed to provide pastoral care to teenagers.

"We need to actually look at why these kids are looking at an online school and actually is it the best option for them," he said.

"If a student's having mental health issues or they're having health issues, is being in your home, in your room, by yourself all day doing this work, is that the best thing for you?"

Abercrombie was also critical of for-profit online schools, which he said had grown in number overseas.

"They're cheap to run. You don't need a building, you don't need to pay for power or oil for the boiler. You don't need to do any of those things so this is a way for businesses, people, organisations to run a school while having the lowest cost possible."

He said the model already existed in the form of Te Kura, The Correspondence School.

"The Correspondence School has that social contract to support public education and this is effectively a private business and so it doesn't have that social contract," he said.

The Charter School Agency provided RNZ with data the school submitted to support its application for growth.

It showed only initial or entry data for reading, writing and maths, but claimed an 82 percent achievement rate for NCEA standards, with a third of results at excellence level.

It also included positive comments from parents and teachers about the school.

World.title: 'Should we be concerned as New Zealanders?' Expert responds to Fiji's HIV emergency
World.content:
A New Zealand traveller planning to visit Fiji on a promotional trip in November says she is waiting for more information after the country declared a national HIV emergency on Tuesday.

The New Zealand government website SafeTravel has warned people travelling to Fiji to avoid activities that could increase their risk of infection.

The traveller, who RNZ Pacific has agreed not to name, said she contacted the organisers of the trip but had yet to receive a response.

She said she is not considering cancelling her trip but wants more information so she can make an informed decision.

"I hope this trip goes ahead without issue," she said.

"But hey, how will we know that someone isn't going to play roulette with our lives?"

RNZ Pacific has sought comment from MediaWorks NZ, which is involved in the promotional trip.

Declaration impact on travellers

University of Canterbury senior health lecturer Dr Jalal Mohammed said the declaration would not be a significant issue for most New Zealanders travelling to Fiji.

However, he told Pacific Waves that it provided a way to reinforce basic health messages.

Fiji HIV crisis: Expert calls for greater regional support Pacific Waves Download MP3 8m

"Should we be concerned as New Zealanders? I mean, we do have strong familial ties with Fiji. A number of our citizens have connections to Fiji, a large number go to Fiji and travel."

"There is a few tourists that will engage in risky behaviours. So I think there is an opportunity to provide key messaging around Fiji is undergoing a HIV epidemic - don't share needles, don't have unprotected sex, those sorts of key messaging."

HIV emergency declaration a 'positive step'

Mohammed said the declaration is a "positive step" in helping the country to tackle the epidemic.

Fiji's government current estimates indicate that one in every 60 adults in Fiji is living with HIV.

Speaking to Pacific Waves, Mohammed said in the past five years the number of HIV cases has increased by 1400 percent.

He said the epidemic is affecting all communites across Fiji, with the pattern of transmission changing as cases continue to climb.

"It's becoming a more generalised outbreak," Mohammed said.

"It is impacting other segments of society so we are seeing sexual transmissions, we are seeing mother-to-child transmissions. So what this declaration does is that it recognises the seriousness of this issue."

Fragile health system

Mohammed said a large portion of Fiji's budget is spent on the country's health system, but that the infrastructure is ailing. He added that discussions of safe needle exchanges need to be actioned.

He added that stigma plays a role in preventing people from accessing treatment.

"There are elements of society that are saying, that if you provide safe needle exchanges, you are promoting drug use - that is not the case."

"We know from evidence that providing safe needle exchanges does not increase drug use but it will certainly decrease the number of cases."



Fiji's development partners could also do a lot more to help the country in its response, Mohammed said.

In July last year, New Zealand gave NZD$4 million to Fiji, but Mohammed said the support should go beyond funding.

He said New Zealand's experience in managing HIV could provide Fiji with technical expertise to help strengthen its response.

World.title: Vanuatu's maritime chief seeks criminal charges over MV Matui disaster
World.content:
Vanuatu authorities seek charges over deadly MV Matui sinking Pacific Waves Download MP3 2m

The Vanuatu Maritime Safety Authority (VMSA) is seeking criminal charges against the captain and owners of the MV Matui.

The VMSA is accusing the owners of Tui Shipping Agency, a company that has reportedly been deregistered since June, of negligence causing deaths of at least two passengers, with the final toll likely to be far more.

Dozens of people remain missing after the inter-island ferry sank off the coast of Vanuatu last Friday.

Vanuatu's Maritime Affairs commissioner Less John Napuati told RNZ Pacific that the authority had never given permission for the vessel to carry passengers.

Napuati said the vessel was only permitted to carry cargo, adding that the MV Matui was issued a specific warning about personnel overflow on 10 September.

"Someone has to be held responsible, and they were saying that it's VMSA that is responsible ... we have to come out and clear our name," he said.

"We issued the appropriate certificate. It's the owner or the master of the vessel that are not complying with the certificate."

The latest casualty estimate for the disaster puts the confirmed death toll at two, though over 30 people are still missing after five days of search and rescue operations.

"It's obvious they caused the death of passengers now," Napuati said.

"So they have to be responsible, held accountable under Section 108 of the Penal Code, and there is also non-compliance of the Shipping Act," noting that it ought to carry prison time for the captain.

It came as Vanuatu Daily Post reported that Tui Shipping Agency had been deregistered as a legal business since 2 June of this year. The company had registered with the Vanuatu Financial Services Commission in March 2024, but had failed to file an annual renewal.

When RNZ Pacific called the company's publicly listed numbers, it found they were each deactivated.

Napuati said he was unaware of this and that it would have been the responsibility of Vanuatu Customs and Inland Revenue (VCIR) to notify his office.

He also said authorisation to carry cargo had been active for the Matui "from 2023 or 2024".

"That's the business side of it, so it's under the jurisdiction of Customs."

The Ministry of the Prime Minister said in a statement on Wednesday that an independent investigation into the MV Matui disaster "will be instigated shortly."

The office "strongly appeals to all families of the victims not to seek revenge or take action outside of the law".

"Let us not create another tragedy on top of this disaster."

World.title: Australia's 43-year MotoGP streak continues with Senna Agius signing
World.content:
There will be a full-time Australian rider in motorcycle racing's premier class for the 43rd consecutive year with 21-year-old Senna Agius signing on to race for KTM Tech3 next year.

The Sydneysider currently sits fourth in the Moto2 standings after placing 10th in 2025.

He has four grand prix wins in Moto2, including at the Circuit of the Americas in the United States and Jerez in Spain earlier this season.

He won his home Moto2 grand prix at Phillip Island last year, and will be in MotoGP for next year's maiden Australian Grand Prix at the new Adelaide street circuit.

Agius has signed on for KTM Tech3, which has former F1 team principal Guenther Steiner has the team's chief executive.

"Today a lifelong dream of mine has come true, reaching MotoGP," Agius said.

"So many years of hard work have gone into this moment and I'm incredibly grateful to Guenther and everyone at Tech3 for believing in me and giving me this opportunity.

"I can't wait to repay their faith. I know the challenge ahead, but I'm ready to learn, work hard, and become the best version of myself with this team."

Australia has had a full-time rider in the premier class since 1985.

In the modern era of grand prix motorcycle racing, which began in 2002 when 500cc two-stroke bikes were replaced with 990cc four-stroke engines, Agius will become the 11th full-time Australian rider.

He will also be the only Australian on the grid next season, with Jack Miller ending his 12-year MotoGP stint and moving to World Superbikes in 2027.

World.title: Alex de Minaur readies for Davis Cup tie between Australia and Poland
World.content:
A Davis Cup tie has come at the perfect time for Alex de Minaur as he searches to recapture a spark after nearly a decade on tour.

The Australian, ranked as high as number five in the world earlier this year, fell to ninth after his shock second-round US Open loss earlier this month.

A quarterfinalist at the Australian Open this year, the 27-year-old has missed golden opportunities to go further in majors since, with Alexander Zverev instead netting two titles as Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz both endured injury-hit seasons.

De Minaur headed straight to Brisbane after his Flushing Meadows disappointment, training with Australian Cup captain Lleyton Hewitt for more than a week before their qualifying tie against Poland begins on Saturday.

De Minaur crashes out of US Open Alex de Minaur has crashed out of the US Open at the second-round stage, beaten in straight sets by Botic van de Zandschulp.

"Back here, around the boys, some good practice, a great team environment; it's been a great little change-up for me," de Minaur said.

"This is exactly what I need to get that spark back that maybe I was missing.

"I've had that spark for 10 years, every single day, right?

"There are stages through your career where things happen, and maybe you don't feel your best. But the timing of this week, it feels like everything's clicking together."

De Minaur has previously taken his losses hard; he copped his most recent defeat to Botic van de Zandschulp with uncharacteristic nonchalance.

But he is adamant the competitive edge remains as he prepares to head a team that includes doubles ace Max Purcell fresh off an 18-month ban for an anti-doping breach.

"Physically I'm great, and mentally I'm in great shape," de Minaur said.

"A rough patch … I've been very fortunate in my career to not have many of those.

"The tennis is still there, mentally there's been matches I haven't played the way I would like.

"But I've got a lot to give, a lot left in the tank, and hopefully I can show it.

"I haven't plateaued in my career. I'm hungry for more and feel I've got the opportunities to achieve it."

De Minaur burst onto the scene when, after being handed a late wildcard, he surged to the Brisbane International semifinals in 2017.

A year later he made his Davis Cup debut at the same venue, losing in a fifth-set tie-break to Zverev.

"I love team competitions … it brings that extra oomph in my game," said de Minaur, who is 17-10 in Davis Cup singles matches.

Poland are without former world number six Hubert Hurkacz, who has skipped the tie as he manages his return from injury, and will be led by world number 73 Kamil Majchrzak.

Rinky Hijikata and Purcell trained together, against Hewitt and de Minaur, at Wednesday's training in a sign they will contest Sunday's doubles tie.

The full draw will be announced on Friday.
